documents.abstract: Abstract This study investigated the correlation between safety awareness and occupational health risk among waste workers in selected government hospitals in Niger-Delta region. Safety awareness was operationalized using modified safety awareness scores while knowledge of occupational health risk exposure was captured using physical factors, biomechanical factors, biological Factors and psychosocial factors. Cross-sectional and inferential designs were adopted. The population comprised hospital waste workers in three selected government hospitals in Niger-Delta States namely Imo, Rivers and Akwa-Ibom State. Data collection was done using questionnaire designed based on a 5-point Likert. Data analysis was done using descriptive statistics and Pearson correlation. The results of the descriptive statistics using weighted average (WA) revealed that knowledge of waste workers on occupational health risk factor is good (WA = 4.09 > 3.00) and the waste workers have substantial level of safety awareness (WA = 3.76>3.00) The Pearson correlation revealed that positive and significant relationship exists between safety awareness, physical factors and psychosocial factors. The results also showed that there is positive but insignificant relationship between safety awareness and biomechanical factor (BMF) however, safety awareness has negative and significant relationship with biological factors (BF). It was therefore concluded that safety awareness has a positive relationship with occupational health risk factors among waste workers in government-owned hospitals in the Niger-Delta. Keywords: Safety Awareness, Occupational health Risk Factors, Waste Workers, Government-owned Hospitals, Niger-delta
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Every week, a university announces a new course on Large Language Models. Every week, a research lab publishes a new paper on LLMs. Every week, a student pays tuition, or signs up for free, to learn how LLMs work. The question this paper asks is simple:Should any of this be happening?Not "is it useful." Not "does it work." Those are different questions, with different answers.The question here is narrower, and sharper:Is there a scientific foundation under the thing being taught and studied?If there is, then yes — teach it, research it, build a discipline. If there isn't, then somethingelse is happening, and we should name it. This paper argues: the foundation is not scientific. And it shows what that means, plainly, with sources.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Objective Guided by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as a conceptual framework, this study explored medical students’ use of large language models (LLMs) in graduation thesis writing, focusing on application patterns, perceptions, and potential risks. Methods A comparative cross-sectional questionnaire survey using convenience sampling was conducted among medical graduates from medical schools in China in 2024 and 2025. The self-designed 25-item questionnaire included five-point Likert items on perceived advantages and disadvantages of LLMs. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's α , exploratory factor analysis (EFA) was performed, and univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were used to identify factors associated with LLMs use. Results A total of 341 valid questionnaires were collected. Overall, 54.25% (185/341) of respondents reported using LLMs in graduation thesis writing, with use reported by 27.37% (52/190) in 2024 and 88.08% (133/151) in 2025. ChatGPT was the most frequently used platform in 2024 (82.69%, 43/52), whereas Deepseek was the most frequently used platform in 2025 (88.72%, 118/133). LLMs were used primarily during the literature review stage (74.05%, 137/185), mainly to provide writing suggestions (82.16%, 152/185). Cronbach's α was 0.720 for perceived advantages and 0.650 for perceived disadvantages, and exploratory factor analysis identified a two-factor clustering pattern consistent with the predefined grouping of perceived advantages and disadvantages. Among LLMs users, 68.65% (127/185) believed that LLMs use would not compromise academic integrity, whereas 47.57% (88/185) remained concerned about potential academic misconduct. The main perceived disadvantages included the risk of academic misconduct, limited content accuracy, and data privacy and security concerns. The findings were discussed with reference to TAM-related concepts as an interpretive framework. Conclusion LLMs use was substantially higher in the 2025 survey than in the 2024 survey. Although LLMs improve writing efficiency and provide valuable writing support, concerns regarding academic integrity, content accuracy, and data privacy remain important considerations. The TAM provides a useful framework for interpreting students’ adoption patterns and may inform the development of AI education and governance strategies in medical education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Enterprise generative artificial intelligence assistants can retrieve organizational information, recommend decisions, and initiate actions through connected tools. These capabilities make cybersecurity a question of how authority and responsibility are distributed across systems and organizations. This study examines how public guidance translates security responsibilities into controls over enterprise AI assistants. A purposive corpus of 12 documentary units from public bodies, a security community, and technology providers was retrieved on 28 September 2026. Focused qualitative document analysis combined six initial coding categories with cross-document comparison, producing a register of 27 evidence records. Four interpretive themes were developed: responsibility is allocated at different organizational and technical levels; permission inheritance requires contextual judgment about appropriate access; human oversight depends on enforceable intervention points; and incident accountability requires continuity across organizational and temporal boundaries. Counterevidence matters: the corpus contains explicit oversight, authorization, and incident-management provisions, so it does not support a general claim that AI security guidance lacks responsibility requirements. The analysis instead identifies an implementation translation problem between broad obligations, application-level controls, and locally assigned decision rights. A proposed governance framework links retrieval, recommendation, and action capabilities to permission boundaries, intervention conditions, accountable owners, and retained decision evidence. The framework is an analytical synthesis, not an empirically validated maturity model. The study contributes a focused account of responsibility at transitions between AI capabilities and offers an auditable structure for enterprise deployment decisions. Its conclusions concern the selected documents and do not establish organizational compliance, control effectiveness, or industry-wide prevalence.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Digital transformation has dissolved the boundaries on which conventional network security was built. Cloud platforms, remote work, mobile endpoints, and the Internet of Things have turned organizational networks into distributed, hyper-connected ecosystems in which the perimeter-based “castle-and-moat” model can no longer separate trusted from untrusted entities. Once inside such a perimeter, adversaries exploit implicit trust to move laterally, and they increasingly use algorithmic tools to automate reconnaissance and attack. At the same time, defensive architectures that depend on pervasive monitoring collide with legal and ethical obligations to protect communication privacy. Within the context of algorithmic transformation, this chapter offers a theoretical evaluation of cybersecurity, network security, and privacy. Drawing on recent literature, standards, and national and international governance frameworks, it examines three interrelated themes: the shift from perimeter defense to Zero Trust Architecture and its operationalization through microsegmentation in virtualized, containerized, and multi-cloud environments; the role of network observability, deep packet inspection, and Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) systems in correlating distributed telemetry; and the dilemma between comprehensive end-to-end monitoring and the preservation of privacy. The analysis shows that continuous verification, least privilege, and an assume-breach posture cannot be enforced through static rules alone; their practical viability depends on artificial intelligence and machine learning that establish behavioral baselines, adjust trust dynamically, synthesize segmentation policies, and orchestrate automated responses through SIEM, Extended Detection and Response (XDR), and Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platforms. The chapter treats privacy as an architectural design constraint rather than a regulatory burden and discusses how Privacy by Design, homomorphic encryption, differential privacy, and federated learning can reconcile intelligent defense with data protection. Its central contribution is a conceptual reconciliation of the security-privacy trade-off: by shifting from payload inspection to encrypted traffic analysis and endpoint-centric telemetry, organizations can retain the visibility that Zero Trust requires without breaking end-to-end encryption. For security governance, this implies that cybersecurity must become a continuous, identity-driven organizational capability. The chapter also identifies the need for empirical validation against adversarial evasion and for explainable, auditable autonomous defense, and it outlines future research on autonomous policy synthesis, post-quantum Zero Trust, edge-native federated telemetry, and formal verification of defensive AI models.

Executive Summary Serbia’s artificial intelligence (AI) landscape is evolving rapidly. It is being shaped by parallel advances in digitalisation, innovation, industrial adoption and emerging regulatory frameworks. In recent years, the country has invested in modernising public services, strengthening its research and innovation capacity, and supporting the growth of high-tech companies and start-ups. These developments have created a foundation for the more systematic and large-scale deployment of AI across key sectors, including Health, Energy, Environment & Sustainability, and Culture & Language domains, where growing technological capabilities and a progressively more mature ecosystem can be developed. The primary objective of this report is to establish an empirical and analytical foundation for positioning Serbian Artificial Intelligence Factory Antenna (SAIFA) as the central national mechanism for integrating the Serbian AI ecosystem into the wider European high-performance computing (Europa) value chain. In strict alignment with the project proposal's description, the deliverable provides a detailed mapping of Serbian AI ecosystem actors, business domains, regulatory drivers, and barriers to adoption, alongside a dedicated focus on four priority verticals: Health, Energy, Environment & Sustainability, and Culture & Language. The report is structured to provide a comprehensive assessment of Serbia’s emerging AI ecosystem, combining desk-based analysis with planned field research. It first presents the methodology applied throughout the assessment, including the main analytical approaches, data sources and criteria used for mapping and evaluating the national AI landscape. The subsequent sections present the findings of the desktop research, including an assessment of the Serbian AI landscape and an analysis of stakeholders relevant to the SAIFA project. The AI landscape assessment covers four key dimensions of the national AI ecosystem: research & education, industry & commercial AI activities, regulatory framework, and computational infrastructure. The stakeholder analysis, in turn, identifies the organization’s and stakeholder groups relevant to SAIFA, examining their roles, capabilities, needs and potential contribution to the project and its activities. Starting in September 2026, the assessment will be complemented by field research involving interviews, surveys and focus groups with different stakeholder groups. This research will provide a more in-depth understanding of the barriers, needs, opportunities and potential for AI development and adoption in Serbia, complementing the evidence gathered through the desktop analysis. The findings from the field research will subsequently be consolidated and disseminated through dedicated thematic SAIFA White Papers, providing evidence-based insights into AI readiness, adoption barriers, user needs and development opportunities in selected areas. The results will also be formally incorporated into Deliverable D2.3, ensuring that the evidence collected through field research feeds directly into the subsequent stages of the SAIFA project. The entire research architecture is designed to remain coherent with international benchmarks and the engagement models of sister European AI Factories, specifically Pharos and IT4LIA, while ensuring strict compliance with General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and data management protocols. Alongside this report, a structured Serbian AI Ecosystem Database was developed, providing a tabular overview of AI-related scientific and research projects, publications by authors affiliated with Serbian institutions, patent applications, study programmes, AI companies, ecosystem enablers, support programmes, regulatory frameworks and regulatory-development initiatives, public institutions, and national AI and computing infrastructure. The database is designed to be made publicly accessible through the SAIFA website and to serve as a living resource that can be regularly updated as the Serbian AI ecosystem evolves. The assessment of macroeconomic and general digital preconditions positions Serbia as a fast-advancing adopter and the leading Western Balkan (WB) economy in AI readiness. This trajectory is underpinned by a highly competitive Information and Communications Technology (ICT) sector, which achieved a record export surplus and an all-time high total export value of €4.55 billion in 2025 (OITEG, 2026). However, a granular evaluation across the four conceptual pillars of the AI ecosystem reveals deep structural asymmetries: · Research, Innovation and Education: Serbia has introduced foundational AI components across primary and secondary curricula and accredited nine specialized AI-focused degree programs since 2021. Scientific publication output has experienced a sharp expansion, exceeding 450 AI-related papers in 2025. Conversely, the commercialization of this knowledge remains a critical bottleneck; only 66 AI-related patent applications were filed between 2017 and mid-2026, highlighting a weak technology-transfer pipeline from academia to market. · Industry and Firm-Level Intensity: The domestic AI business landscape comprises approximately 300 developers and integrators. Startups and Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises (SMEs) form the dominant core, accounting for 89% of these firms, showcasing high agility and an entrepreneurial drive that culminated in the emergence of Serbia’s first tech unicorn (Ominimo) in 2026. However, the corporate and venture capital layers are thin. Venture capital (VC) expenditure stands at a critical low of 8.0% of the EU average, leaving the startup base heavily reliant on public grants and personal funds, which severely restricts their ability to scale commercially. · Regulation and Governance: Serbia has actively established strategic policy intent, moving from its initial Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia (SDAIRS) (2020–2025) and Ethical Guidelines to a comprehensive new SDAIRS for the Period 2025–2030. In the absence of specialized legislation, AI is currently governed by a distributed matrix of horizontal laws (data protection, cybersecurity, non-discrimination). The upcoming draft Law on Artificial Intelligence, largely aligned with the EU AI Act, signals Serbia’s move towards a more comprehensive AI regulatory framework. · Computational Infrastructure: Serbia’s computational infrastructure is developing rapidly, with significant investments in national AI and High-Performance Computing (HPC) capacity. Hosted at the Government Data Center in Kragujevac (GDCK), the National AI Platform has reached a combined operational capacity of 37 PFLOPS using NVIDIA A100 and H200 GPU architectures. The planned delivery of a third supercomputer based on NVIDIA Grace Hopper technology in early 2027 will further strengthen Serbia’s national AI and computing capacity. This report also provides a systematic Stakeholder Analysis, categorising ecosystem actors according to their functional roles within the AI ecosystem. The analysis distinguishes four main groups: Data Providers and Domain Experts (public institutions, utilities and industrial organisations holding valuable datasets and domain knowledge), AI Researchers and Model Developers (universities and research institutes providing methodological and machine-learning expertise), AI Application Developers (startups and software companies turning AI capabilities into applications), and End-Users and Beneficiaries (e.g. patients, farmers, businesses and public administrations whose needs define the objectives of AI solutions). The analysis is complemented by cross-cutting ecosystem enablers and intermediaries, including science and technology parks, industry associations, chambers, incubators and accelerators, as well as investors, funding organisations and public authorities. Their role is particularly important for matchmaking, dissemination, funding, regulation and creating the conditions for collaboration. Sector-specific analyses were conducted for healthcare, energy, environment & sustainability, and language & culture, identifying relevant stakeholder groups, concrete organisations, and the resources they can contribute or require. Illustrative use cases, presented in this section, demonstrate how organisations with complementary data, domain expertise, AI capabilities and market access can be connected through SAIFA. The analysis therefore proposes stakeholder engagement activities focused on turning connections into concrete projects, including thematic workshops and roundtables, AI-focused forums and hackathons, direct outreach and bilateral meetings, SAIFA information sessions, and participation in sector-specific and scientific events. Together, these activities position SAIFA not only as an AI and HPC service provider, but as a facilitator of collaboration, resource exchange and joint solution development across Serbia’s AI ecosystem. Serbia’s strongest AI potential lies in HealthTech and BioTech, as well as in environment and sustainability, where established research capacities, relevant data, industry demand and an emerging base of technology providers provide a solid foundation for further development. At the same time, culture & language, as well as cybersecurity, represent emerging high-potential areas, characterised by a growing number of AI-related projects, research activities and companies, although their ecosystem bases are currently less developed. These areas therefore offer significant opportunities for targeted ecosystem-building and are particularly relevant to SAIFA’s project priorities. The ecosystem is geographically concentrated around Belgrade, Novi Sad, Niš and Kragujevac, with major Research and Development (R&D) and computing capacities centred on leading universities, research institutes and national infrastructure. documents.abstract: Executive Summary Context. The Serbian AI Factory Antenna (SAIFA) is a HORIZON-JU-EuroHPC project (Grant Agreement No. 101263280) that establishes a national entry point to artificial intelligence and high-performance computing for research and clinical institutions, industry, the public sector and individual users. The AI Gateway is developed in Work Package 3, Task 3.4, as the unified access point for AI resources, tools and services. Deliverable D3.1, due in M03, provides the comprehensive initial plan for its development. Scope. The design covers access to computing environments, datasets, pre-trained models, applications, reusable tools, modular workflows, training materials and support services. It also addresses authentication, resource scheduling, monitoring, secure sharing and interoperability with national infrastructure, Pharos, IT4LIA, the AI-on-Demand Platform and other AI Factory services. The design sets out a target direction and an evaluation process. It does not predetermine the final implementation scope, architecture or division of responsibilities, nor does it commit the project consortium to delivering every described capability or workflow in the beta or subsequent releases. Design approach. The Gateway is conceived as a modular integration and control layer rather than a monolithic platform. Mature components are reused for identity management, cataloguing, notebooks, model management, execution, storage, monitoring and learning. SAIFA-specific development is concentrated on the unified portal, common metadata and authorisation rules, quota and accounting logic, the HPC bridge, audit, and federation adapters. Users and use cases. The functional scope is illustrated through 21 Domain Use Stories covering language and culture, biomedicine and health, energy and manufacturing, environment, and cross-domain adoption. A representative set of system use cases specifies the principal interactions for authentication, discovery, data and model management, compute jobs, inference, experiments, training, federation and support. These descriptions remain subject to validation and prioritisation with domain owners, infrastructure operators and user-support teams. Technology and risk. Candidate technologies are evaluated through short proofs of concept, mandatory elimination criteria and comparative assessment of usability, integration effort, operational complexity, performance, maturity, compliance and sustainability. The accompanying risk register combines proposal-level risks with Gateway-specific security, integration, data-integrity and operational risks, and links them to preventive controls and acceptance evidence. Roadmap. The contractual path is D3.1 in M03, access to national infrastructure in M03, access and use policies and the online beta version in M12, and D3.4 - AI gateway functionalities and features - in M18. Task 3.4 continues through M36, covering further integration, hardening, interoperability, validation and operational improvement. Development and preliminary testing are carried out on the PARADOX and ITE infrastructures, followed by validation and benchmarking using the Greek and Italian AI Factory infrastructures. Outcome. Together, these documents form a coherent design baseline that links the project structure, domain needs, system behaviour, candidate technologies, delivery plan and risk controls. The baseline supports implementation while preserving the flexibility needed to incorporate validated user requirements and evidence from the planned proofs of concept.

Precision agriculture (PA) leverages modern technologies to enhance productivity, optimize resource use, and reduce environmental impact. Efficient data management and integration play a critical role in PA, as large volumes of data are generated through Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, remote sensing, geographic information systems (GIS), and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven analytics. This chapter explores various methodologies used to manage, integrate, and utilize agricultural data effectively, emphasizing cloud computing, blockchain, and decision support systems (DSS). We discuss the challenges and future directions of data-driven agriculture to promote sustainability and efficiency. In recent years, a wide range of technologies has been integrated into PA to enhance crop monitoring and management. These advancements aim to improve sustainability while maximizing yield and quality. However, many available technologies and standards have yet to be fully incorporated into these practices. As a result, the potential synergy between breeding and agronomic expertise, electronics, and computing has not been entirely realized. Emerging and established technologies, such as the Internet of Everything (IoE), IoT, cloud and fog computing, alongwith cost-effective, low-power computing devices, and wireless communication methods, have made it possible to rapidly develop and implement innovative monitoring solutions. These technological trends have accelerated the integration of data as a key component in agricultural decision-making, bridging the gap between raw crop data and actionable insights.

Background Occupational accidents in open-pit mining remain a significant workplace safety and public health concern due to hazardous environmental conditions, high-risk tasks, and complex human–organizational interactions. Data-driven risk modeling may enhance accident prevention and occupational health management. Objective To identify key determinants of occupational accidents in an open-pit coal mining operation and develop a predictive risk assessment model to support injury prevention and safety decision-making. Methods A retrospective quantitative study was conducted using accident records (2017–2024) from a large open-pit mining company. Variables included accident timing, location, department, job position, age, work experience, unsafe acts, unsafe conditions, personal factors, and job-related factors. Multivariate regression and artificial neural network (ANN) modeling were applied to examine associations and predict the number of affected workers. Model performance was evaluated using correlation coefficients, mean squared error (MSE), mean absolute deviation (MAD), mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), and bias. Results Unsafe acts, hazardous environments, low worker motivation, and inadequate supervision were dominant risk contributors. Regression analysis showed significant associations between accident variables and injury occurrence ( p < 0.05). The ANN model demonstrated strong predictive performance (overall R = 0.973; testing R = 0.992) with low error (MSE = 0.015; MAPE = 13.2%), while the linear regression model explained comparatively little variance ( R 2 = 0.094), indicating that occupational risk in this setting is driven predominantly by nonlinear interactions among behavioral, environmental, and organizational factors. Accidents were more frequent among operators, workers aged 26–30 years, and employees with >5 years of experience. Conclusions Integrating statistical and machine learning approaches provides a structured framework for identifying occupational risk patterns. Predictive modeling can support targeted supervision, behavioral safety interventions, and hazard control strategies in high-risk industrial settings.

The revolutionized paradigm of Artificial Intelligence (AI), presently gripping the world of marketing, is experiencing a paradigm shift in customer-centric models of marketing around the globe. Artificial Intelligence has transformed the world of marketing by optimizing processes, turbocharging growth, and redefining the future of businesses; thus, experiencing an unprecedented advancement in digital transformations. Notwithstanding the rapid adaptation of AI in businesses, corporations continue experiencing challenging circumstances to derive maximum efficiency out of AI effectively. To derive maximum benefits out of AI effectively, marketers need to identify appropriate use cases that need effective implementation on an execution level. In utilitarian considerations, customers are obsessed with tangible and functional characteristics of products or services. Utilitarian gains happen to be the prime motivators of purchasing decisions that focus on efficiency and often on cost economies. Also, utilitarian practices can trace their roots back to the pleasure principle that is generally recognized as being the best for most people; however, their approach towards accomplishing an enjoyable experience for people works far from an emotional goal and concentrates on functional values related to a product or a service that possesses demand and appeal just like a consumer product needing emphasis on functional values rather than a mere demand that just needs basic attention and focus on a product or a service that needs appreciation related to utility rather than a mere product of utility. Products that assist customers save time or space or result in decreasing costs of products or eliminate daily challenges can increase their utility values of the product itself since customers can identify the products as ‘daily essentials.’ Hedonistic consumption practices focus on engaging with and getting influenced from sensory engagements on a positive product that is seen reeling on imaginative levels of a product where hedonic values are most seen related to products that focus on customers seeing maximum importance related to their utilization of products that concentrate on user needs rather than their utility levels. Very many corporations are increasingly leveraging technological innovations of machine learning-related natural language processing and other AI-related technologies to provide appropriate real-time recommendations to customers that work on AI recommendations a lot being adopted on an unprecedented scale by corporations to assist customers on improving their satisfaction levels. Also, public interest sectors or units are increasingly adopting AI recommendations to assist their customers effectively to get directed towards necessary services. Support on AI recommendations alone won’t attract customers on more fruitful deals. In this paper, I am interested in the effectiveness of AI suggestions in both utilitarian and hedonic products and to what extent the word of machine can affect marketing strategies of corporations for gaining a competitive advantage.

Detecting aircraft engine types has a wide range of applications in both defense and civilian sectors. In military settings, identifying the engine type of an aircraft helps distinguish between passenger platforms and potential threats, enabling appropriate situational response. Recognizing the aircraft category from its acoustic signature is also crucial for real-time situational awareness and sound-based monitoring. On the civilian side, airports and urban authorities use acoustic identification to monitor overhead aircraft, manage air traffic, and assess environmental noise impacts. In this study, we propose a deep learning–based model to classify aircraft into four categories: passenger airplane, drone, fighter jet, and helicopter. Log-frequency cepstral coefficients (LFCCs) are extracted as input features and fed into a custom hybrid architecture combining Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) layers. To evaluate performance, we applied 5-fold cross-validation and compared the proposed model with several baselines, including standard CNN, CNN-LSTM, CNN-GRU, CNN-RNN, and Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifiers. Experimental results show that our model outperforms all baselines in classification accuracy. The proposed model achieved an overall accuracy of 82.65% for the four-class task. After applying temporal consistency smoothing as a post-processing step, overall accuracy improved to 83.40%, with passenger airplane accuracy increasing from 70.7% to 73.44% and fighter accuracy from 81.5% to 84.62%. The binary engine-type classification task achieved 84.15% accuracy, which remained unchanged after smoothing. An ablation study confirmed the synergistic effect of combining CNN and LSTM components, as the CNN-only and LSTM-only models achieved only 61.4% and 53.9% accuracy, respectively.

The rapid growth of digital data and the increasing complexity of security threats have expanded the use of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning in modern security systems. This chapter presents the conceptual foundations of deep learning and pattern recognition and examines their roles in security-oriented applications. It first clarifies the relationships among artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, and pattern recognition, emphasizing the transition from manually engineered features to representation learning through multilayer neural networks. Fundamental mechanisms of deep learning, including artificial neurons, activation functions, forward propagation, backpropagation, loss functions, and hierarchical representation learning, are subsequently discussed. The chapter also reviews major deep learning architectures, including Multilayer Perceptrons, Convolutional Neural Networks, Recurrent Neural Networks, Long Short-Term Memory networks, Autoencoders, and Transformers, with particular attention to their suitability for different data types and security problems. Their applications are examined in the context of intrusion detection, anomaly detection, malware detection, phishing detection, security log analysis, and physical and biometric security. Recent developments involving large language models, federated learning, Edge AI, and continual learning are also considered as emerging directions for security analysis. Beyond predictive performance, the chapter emphasizes that reliable artificial intelligence-based security systems must address several limitations and risks. These include data quality and representativeness, class imbalance, overfitting, data and concept drift, adversarial attacks, data poisoning, model extraction, and membership inference attacks. The discussion further highlights the importance of explainability, privacy, algorithmic fairness, robustness, and human oversight, particularly in high-risk security environments where incorrect decisions may have significant consequences. Overall, the chapter argues that artificial intelligence and security have a bidirectional relationship: artificial intelligence can strengthen threat detection and decision support, while AI systems themselves may become targets of malicious manipulation. Future security systems are therefore expected to rely increasingly on trustworthy, explainable, privacy-aware, adaptive, and human-supervised approaches that combine advanced pattern recognition capabilities with operational and ethical safeguards.

This paper demonstrates an EEG-based machine learning system of automated depression detection using the publicly available dataset of BRMH EEG data. The information is in the form of multi-channel power spectral density and coherence of different psychiatric disorders, mood disorders, anxiety, schizophrenia, and healthy controls. Numerous preprocessing and feature standardization and Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) were used to deal with missing data and the issue of class imbalance. Three classifiers were developed and tested K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) and Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Random Forest (RF); they were trained and tested on ten-fold stratified cross-validations using weighted accuracy, precision, recall and F1-scores. Of these, the Random Forest model performed best of all with an average accuracy of 92.6 with and without showing its ability to predict nonlinear EEG features relationship. KNN attained moderate outcomes, and SVM failed because of the dimension of data. The results point to the practicability of EEG biomarkers and ensemble learning in the exact and non- invasive detection of depression that would be used in the future in the development of deep learning and multimodal fusion to support clinical decisions.

documents.abstract: In this study, the design and control of a mobile gardening robot based on image processing and artificial intelligence were implemented. The system, running on Raspberry Pi 4B, can distinguish different plant species and weeds using a YOLOv5-based object detection and classification model; it performs tasks such as cutting weeds, watering useful plants, and moving autonomously while avoiding obstacles. Experiments conducted in a pot environment demonstrated that the robot can successfully perform plant detection, classification, and maintenance functions. With these features, the developed robot offers a low-cost and sustainable solution for small and medium-scale agricultural businesses. The mobile gardening robot designed within the scope of the study was experimentally tested for image processing-based plant recognition, autonomous plant orientation, plant cutting, and watering operations for different scenarios. When the results obtained were examined, it was seen that the developed deep learning-based plant detection model achieved an 82% mAP@50 success rate, while the plant classification model achieved a 92.9% mAP@50 success rate.

Auxetic structures, with a negative Poisson’s ratio, have gained significant attention for aerospace and automotive applications due to their superior mechanical performance. In this study, two different Auxetic Structures were used, namely Re–entrant Hexagon (A) and Re-entrant star triangular structure (B). They were designed and fabricated with the use of Stereolithography (SLA) Additive Manufacturing with the use of Standard Photopolymer Resin Material. The mechanical Behaviour was investigated with the help of compression testing according to ASTM D695 Standards using a Universal Testing Machine (UTM). These findings confirm that Auxetic geometry strongly influences mechanical behaviour and performance. The namely Re–entrant Hexagon (A) Geometry is better suited for Flexible and cushioning applications, such as biomedical devices used in implants, ergonomic materials, shoe soles, and soft protective paddings, while the Re- entrant Star triangular (B) geometry is suitable for applications requiring High Strength and Impact Resistance, such as aerospace Sandwich Structures, automotive crash absorbers, and protective equipment.

Purpose: This article develops a Human Governed Agentic Project Management (HG-APM) model for integrating autonomous AI capabilities with human project management authority. Design/methodology/approach: An integrative conceptual synthesis combines four literature streams: AI-enabled project management, autonomous Manager Agents, human oversight governance, and human–AI teaming. Source supported findings are separated from conceptual inferences, and the resulting architecture is expressed as a closed-loop model. Findings: The model comprises Sense, Understand, Diagnose, Predict, Plan, Evaluate, Authorize, Act, Monitor, Learn and Replan. It proposes a consequence sensitive, graduated autonomy rather than a single autonomy level. Routine and reversible actions may be automated within predefined boundaries, whereas consequential financial, contractual, scope, safety, stakeholder, reputational and strategic decisions require stronger authority from the designated human or organizational decisionmaker. Originality: The model integrates project-management intelligence, human–AI teaming and governance into one operational architecture. It contributes to a project specific decision boundary and testable propositions for evaluating whether governed agentic AI improves project outcomes without weakening human control.

documents.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly embedded in online and blended higher education, pressing assumptions about authorship, academic integrity, and transparency are being re-examined, raising urgent questions for the transformation of the teaching and learning environment. While existing studies document students’ attitudes toward AI and general AI literacy, fewer instruments assess students’ self-reported understanding of responsible academic AI use. This study reports the development and preliminary validation of the Responsible AI Use Knowledge Scale (RAUKS) for college students in teacher education. Guided conceptually by the 6Cs approach as an item-development heuristic, an initial 46-item pool was administered to 410 undergraduate students. Exploratory structural equation modeling (ESEM) supported a refined 24-item instrument with a three-factor structure: Ethical Normative Knowledge (ENK), Critical Corrective Knowledge (CCK), and Procedural Disclosure Knowledge (PDK). The three-factor solution explained 61.67% of the total variance and demonstrated excellent model fit (χ² (230) = 364, p < .001, RMSEA = .038, SRMR = .033, CFI = .999, TLI = .999). Internal consistency reliability was strong across factors (ω = .97 for ENK, .84 for CCK, and .81 for PDK). The results provide initial evidence that responsible AI use perceived knowledge is multidimensional, comprising integrity-related expectations, critical evaluation of AI outputs, and disclosure procedures. RAUKS contributes a knowledge-focused self-report assessment tool offering practical utility for diagnosing student preparedness, informing instructional design, and supporting integrity-oriented AI policies. Further cross-validation across institutions, programs, and modalities is recommended.

documents.abstract: The proliferation of mobile technologies has fundamentally transformed how library services are delivered and accessed. This paper examines the development of mobile applications for library access and user interaction, synthesizing recent research on design methodologies, user needs analysis, implementation strategies, and evaluation approaches. Drawing on case studies and empirical research from diverse institutional contexts, the paper identifies key trends including user-centred design frameworks, the integration of artificial intelligence capabilities, and the imperative of addressing underserved communities. The analysis reveals that successful library mobile applications must balance essential functional requirements such as catalogue searching and account management with attractive features that enhance user engagement. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions and practical recommendations for libraries undertaking mobile application development initiatives.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into Islamic Religious Education (PAI) offers opportunities to develop innovative learning media that support students' spiritual education. This study aims to develop AI-based animation media adapted from Hamzah Fansuri's Syair Sidang Ahli Suluk and examine students' responses to its use as a medium for spiritual education. The research employed a Research and Development (R&D) approach using the ADDIE model, comprising analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation. The development process transformed Sufistic values into narratives, characters, dialogues, and animated visuals contextualized within students' everyday experiences. The product was reviewed by Islamic Religious Education content experts and Visual Communication Design media experts. A limited trial involving 50 students at ISBI Aceh employed a 20-item response questionnaire using a five-point Likert scale. The findings revealed positive student responses, with an overall mean score of 3.87 (77.47%). Spiritual awareness received the highest score of 4.07 (81.30%), whereas self-reflection recorded the lowest score of 3.77 (75.38%). These findings suggest that AI-based animation offers potential for contextualizing the Sufistic intellectual heritage of the Indonesian archipelago within students' digital experiences. The study contributes to integrating Sufistic values, students' lived experiences, and audiovisual technology into Islamic spiritual education. However, the findings reflect students' acceptance and perceptions rather than causal evidence of improved spirituality. Further research is therefore necessary to examine the effectiveness of this media in fostering spiritual value internalization through more comprehensive and longitudinal assessments.

Background: Due to rapid digitalization, there is a complete change in the teaching and learning strategies. Even though digitalization provides flexibility and accessibility to learning but long-term digital engagement has led to growing concerns about digital burnout and emotional cognitive and physical exhaustion especially in early year university students. This review aims to map the available evidence on digital burnout among early-year university students. The aim of this review is to compile the recent research on the concepts, associated factors, consequences and gaps in literature on digital burnout among early year university students. Methods: A thorough search was done using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and Google Scholar to find studies published between January 2010 and October 2025 on digital burnout. All review and empirical works that addressed digital fatigue, technostress, and burnout in higher education were included. Synthesis of literature: Several studies point out that prolonged digital exposure caused emotional exhaustion decreased motivation and cognitive fatigue. These features were categorized as indicators of digital burnout. Early year university students are at a high risk of digital burnout mainly because of their limited coping mechanisms difficulties in managing time and adjusting to digital learning environments. These students are suddenly exposed to high academic workload and social isolation which leads to overuse of screens. These can lead to various implications like decreased academic engagement, psychological distress, and impaired concentration. There is mention of coping mechanisms in several studies that include time management, digital detoxes, mindfulness, and institutional support through counselling and hybrid learning programs. Conclusion: In higher education, digital burnout is an increasingly prevalent issue. But this area needs to be further explored. To improve resilience, measures need to be taken at various levels including organization, family, peers and self. Universities should include more human factors, provide self-regulation training, and education on digital well-being in first-year orientation programs. To better elucidate causative factors and evaluate the effectiveness of preventive measures, future cross-cultural, discipline-specific studies need to be conducted.

Background: Digital health and artificial intelligence (AI) are rapidly transforming rehabilitation practice, creating an urgent need for rehabilitation professionals to develop new competencies through continuing professional development (CPD). Despite the growing importance of digital rehabilitation, evidence regarding digital health and AI-related CPD needs among rehabilitation professionals in low- and middle-income countries remains limited. This study aimed to identify the digital health and AI-related CPD needs of rehabilitation professionals in Jordan. Methods: A national convergent parallel mixed-methods study was conducted between January and May 2026. Licensed physiotherapists, occupational therapists, speech-language therapists, and prosthetists/orthotists completed a structured online questionnaire assessing CPD participation, digital health competencies, AI-related knowledge, perceived barriers, and future educational priorities. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with a purposive sample of rehabilitation professionals and key stakeholders to further explore experiences and educational needs. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, while qualitative data underwent reflexive thematic analysis. Findings from both components were integrated during interpretation. Results: A total of 462 rehabilitation professionals completed the survey, and 20 participated in qualitative interviews. Artificial intelligence (mean = 4.71 ± 0.52), telerehabilitation (4.64 ± 0.61), clinical decision support systems (4.59 ± 0.65), and virtual reality rehabilitation (4.55 ± 0.69) emerged as the highest-priority CPD topics. Among the 462 participants, 169 (36.6%) reported previous participation in digital-health-related CPD, while 82 (17.7%) reported receiving formal education in artificial intelligence. The principal barriers to CPD participation were lack of time (84.4%), financial cost (79.2%), limited AI-focused educational opportunities (76.8%), and inadequate employer support (63.0%). Previous digital health training, years of professional experience, and employer support independently predicted higher self-reported digital health competency (adjusted R2 = 0.39; p < 0.05). Qualitative findings demonstrated that rehabilitation professionals recognized digital transformation as inevitable but reported insufficient practical training, organisational support, and nationally coordinated educational opportunities. Conclusions: Jordanian rehabilitation professionals demonstrated high motivation to develop competencies in digital health and AI but reported substantial educational and organisational barriers. National competency frameworks, structured CPD programmes, and integration of digital health into rehabilitation curricula are needed to prepare the rehabilitation workforce for technology-enabled healthcare. The findings may inform workforce development strategies in Jordan and other low- and middle-income countries undergoing digital transformation.

documents.abstract: Digital transformation in healthcare, driven by the widespread adoption of electronic health records, the growth of large-scale health data, the expansion of telehealth applications, and advances in data-processing capacity, is strengthening the role of artificial intelligence within healthcare systems. Technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and generative artificial intelligence are increasingly used in diagnosis and screening, clinical decision support, personalized care, patient monitoring, workflow optimization, and the improvement of access to healthcare services. This chapter provides a comprehensive conceptual and narrative review of the effects of artificial intelligence on healthcare services and health economics. It examines the impact of AI on diagnostic accuracy, early detection, clinical decision-making, healthcare professionals’ workload, service capacity, workforce productivity, access, and equity. In addition, the economic value of AI applications is evaluated in terms of cost-effectiveness, cost-benefit, resource allocation, reimbursement mechanisms, health technology assessment, and implementation costs. Existing evidence indicates that AI can accelerate diagnostic processes, reduce unnecessary procedures and tests, improve the utilization of healthcare professionals and high-cost medical equipment, and generate cost-effective outcomes in specific applications. However, the economic value of AI is not uniform across healthcare systems or areas of application. Patient volume, workforce costs, existing infrastructure, licensing and integration expenses, maintenance and updating costs, reimbursement structures, and institutional characteristics of healthcare systems substantially influence economic outcomes. Ethical and regulatory issues, including data security, algorithmic bias, explainability, clinical accountability, human oversight, and equity in access to healthcare, are also critical to the sustainable adoption of AI technologies. Overall, the value of artificial intelligence in healthcare should not be assessed solely on the basis of technical performance or short-term cost savings. A comprehensive assessment should consider clinical outcomes, economic value, implementation conditions, human–AI collaboration, ethical responsibilities, and long-term sustainability together.

documents.abstract: Introduction Machine translation and generative artificial intelligence (AI) are now common resources in English as a foreign language learning, yet evidence from Latin American higher education remains limited and often conflates tool use with learning impact. This study characterized translation practices, tool preferences, print-dictionary use, and AI-assisted text revision among university students in southern Peru. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 435 students from 37 degree programs and seven faculties at a public university. Questionnaire items were analyzed as separate indicators rather than combined into a latent scale. Valid percentages with 95% Wilson confidence intervals were estimated, paired exact McNemar tests were used for within-participant comparisons, faculty differences were assessed using Monte Carlo chi-square tests with false-discovery-rate adjustment, and an exploratory logistic regression was fitted. Results Use of AI or automated translators was reported by 94.7% of respondents, and 92.4% used translation applications or websites. Both were more prevalent than print-dictionary experience (65.4%; paired odds ratios 9.86 and 7.88, respectively; both p < .001). Google Translate predominated across questionnaire contexts, whereas ChatGPT accounted for 7.7% of responses to the general-use item and 34.0% to the AI-focused item. AI-assisted revision was reported by 74.1% and varied across faculties (52.2%-96.8%; Cramér's V = .274, q < .001). Although 75.0% reported using print dictionaries rarely or never, 78.0% supported their continued promotion. Discussion The findings describe a heterogeneous institutional translation ecology in which widespread digital-tool adoption coexists with disciplinary variation, context-dependent tool preferences, and continued endorsement of print resources. These findings do not establish learning effects. They support pedagogical attention to verification, post-editing, and independent language production, whose effectiveness requires direct evaluation.

Digital Twin (DT) technology is rapidly evolving from a digital representation of physical assets into a decision-support infrastructure that integrates real-time data, analytics, and simulation. However, existing research remains fragmented across application domains, limiting understanding of how DTs enable decision-making under different socio-technical conditions. This study presents a systematic literature review and decision-centric comparative analysis of DT applications in two contrasting decision environments: Supply Chain Management (SCM) and healthcare. Following a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) protocol, 193 peer-reviewed studies (95 SCM and 98 healthcare) were identified, screened, and synthesized across six analytical dimensions: application domains, technological integration, decision-making levels, business value, stakeholder involvement, and implementation challenges. The findings reveal fundamentally different decision logics despite a shared technological foundation based on Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and cloud computing. SCM-DTs primarily support coordination, optimization, resilience, and organizational scalability, whereas healthcare-DTs emphasize personalization, patient safety, and ethical governance under stringent regulatory constraints. Building on these findings, the study proposes a decision-centric comparative framework and a value–complexity perspective suggesting that value realization is increasingly associated with technological, organizational, and governance complexity as DT ecosystems mature. The paper advances the conceptualization of DTs as socio-technical decision systems and provides practical guidance for researchers, managers, and policymakers seeking responsible and effective digital transformation.

documents.abstract: Safety-incident reports are written with deliberate epistemic caution: A reporter marks what was seen, what was inferred, and what remains unsure, and a dropped hedge can turn a tentative observation into an apparent cause. As large language models take over summarizing such reports for triage, indexing, and search, whether they preserve that caution becomes a property of the safety record itself. This study asks whether models keep a reporter's expressed uncertainty when they summarize, testing two hypotheses fixed before any summary was generated: that models systematically harden uncertainty by default and that an explicit instruction to preserve it overcorrects into softening. Six open-weight models summarized 42 real incident reports, 30 from the United States Aviation Safety Reporting System and 12 from the United Kingdom Marine Accident Investigation Branch, under a plain prompt, a preserve prompt, and a paraphrase of it. Uncertainty change was measured two ways: at the passage level, by a deterministic epistemic-marker lexicon, and at the claim level, by aligning those markers between source and summary, each validated against manual annotation and cross-checked against two independent language-model judges. Under plain summarization, all six models hardened the reporter's uncertainty (claim-level hardening 0.59–0.85), dropping explicit hedges almost entirely (retention about 0.08) while epistemic modal verbs survived far better. The preserve instruction reversed the pattern into over-softening: In a cluster-robust logistic regression, it carried an odds ratio of 0.12 (95% CI [0.03, 0.49], p = 0.003) and held once summary length was controlled, so the change reflects expressed certainty rather than compression. In practical terms, the instruction lowered the predicted probability of hardening from about 0.43 to 0.13 (Cohen's h = 0.69), and the effect held in mixed-effects models and under adverse imputation of the missing outputs. The pattern was directionally consistent across the tested models and both instruction wordings. Automated safety triage that relies on model summaries should measure epistemic fidelity directly and not treat a single preserve instruction as a solution.

Against the backdrop of the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence technologies, traditional design value assessment systems based on creative input are facing new challenges. This study aims to examine the effects of design source (human-designed design vs. AI-assisted design), design style (commercial style vs. AI-native style), and campaign duration on the value assessment of design works in the AI era. Drawing on a real e-commerce platform context, the study conducts empirical analyses through two multifactor experiments. Experiment 1 adopts a 2 × 5 mixed experimental design to compare the value assessment performance of human-designed and AI-assisted design works across different campaign durations. Experiment 2 further introduces the variable of design style and employs a 2 × 2 × 5 three-factor experimental design to investigate the interaction effects among design source, design style, and campaign duration. The findings indicate that AI-assisted design demonstrates significant efficiency advantages in terms of time and cost. However, regarding value assessment indicators such as number of clicks, click-through rate (CTR), conversion rate (CVR), and sales performance, AI-assisted design performs comparably to human-designed design overall. Different design styles exhibit stage-specific differences: commercial style is more effective in attracting user attention and promoting conversion during the early stage of campaigns, whereas AI-native style gradually demonstrates higher conversion efficiency and cost advantages in the middle and later stages. In addition, the value assessment of design works exhibits significant temporal dynamics, with advertising performance reaching a relatively optimal level during the middle stage of campaign deployment. The study finds that AI significantly reduces creative input without weakening the market performance of design works, providing new evidence for understanding the input–outcome relationship in design value. The study also offers practical insights for enterprises seeking to optimize collaborative creation strategies between AI and human designers. Cervical and lumbar spondylosis are common degenerative spinal disorders associated with musculoskeletal pain, disability, and reduced work productivity. Where age is a major risk factor, occupational and ergonomic exposures contribute to spinal degeneration. Repetitive biomechanical loading and heavy lifting may accelerate degenerative changes. This narrative review aims to understand the dose- response relationship between occupational and ergonomic factors, development of cervical and lumbar spondylosis, while evaluating dose-response patterns that are associated with pharmacological, rehabilitative and ergonomic interventions. A narrative review of available literature was conducted on occupational risk factors, ergonomic determinants, cumulative biomechanical loading, pathophysiological and therapeutic strategies related to cervical and lumbar spondylosis. Evidence related to exposure intensity, frequency, duration and treatment outcomes were synthesized. Occupational exposures contribute to spinal degeneration through chronic mechanical overload, repetitive microtrauma, impaired disc nutrition and progressive structural deterioration. Increasing intensity, frequency, and duration of occupational exposure are associated with greater risks of cervical and lumbar spondylosis. Prolonged heavy lifting, repetitive bending, prolonged sitting, and vibration are associated with increased disc degeneration and functional impairment. Pharmacological therapies including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, muscle relaxants, neuropathic agents provide symptomatic relief, while physiotherapy, ergonomic rehabilitation exhibit dose-dependent clinical responses and offer more sustainable long-term improvements. Occupational and ergonomic factors plays major role in development and progression of cervical and lumbar spondylosis, with greater exposure greater the risk. Early ergonomic intervention, appropriate rehabilitation and individualized treatment improve function and minimize occupational disability.

Purpose: This paper describes the design and operation of DriftAgent, a system that detects configuration drift in Terraform-managed cloud infrastructure and prepares fixes for human review. It also reports what we learned from running the system in production at a streaming television company. Methodology: The study used a single-site case study design to evaluate a production deployment. DriftAgent runs every weekday morning: it asks an Atlantis server to plan 187 Terraform projects in parallel, parses the plan output, and sends each drifted project, together with its source files, to a large language model in a single request. The model returns HCL changes, including Terraform import blocks for resources that exist in the cloud but not in state; the agent opens a GitLab merge request for human review and posts a daily summary to Slack. Over twelve weeks (56 runs), we measured four outcomes: the fate of each merge request (merged unchanged, merged after edits, or closed), plan sweep time, engineering time per drift event, and inference cost. Merge request outcomes were validated by two engineers who independently rated a random sample of 120 merge requests as acceptable, acceptable with edits, or unacceptable against defined criteria, and inter-rater reliability was measured with Cohen’s kappa. Engineering effort was compared with a pre-deployment timing study of 71 manually handled drift events. Data were analyzed with descriptive statistics (counts, percentages, means, medians, and 95th percentiles), edited or closed proposals were classified by their main failure reason, and the findings were synthesized by triangulating production logs, merge request histories, the independent ratings, and the timing data. Findings: Across 56 runs the system recorded 372 drift events and opened 351 merge requests. Reviewers merged 73.5% of them without semantic changes and 18.2% after edits, and closed 8.3%. Moving plan execution from a sequential loop to Atlantis reduced the median sweep time from 52.0 to 11.4 minutes. Weekly engineering time spent on drift fell from 9.4 to 2.4 hours, at an inference cost of about US$0.08 per drifted project. The most common reasons for edited or rejected proposals were choosing the wrong kind of remediation and formatting an import identifier incorrectly. Unique contribution to theory, practice and policy: The study gives evidence that a fixed workflow with one model call, a deterministic plan check, and mandatory human approval is a workable way to use language models in change-controlled infrastructure. For practitioners, it documents specific design choices and failure modes. For organizations writing policy on AI in operations, it supports keeping approval and apply rights with people while assigning analysis and drafting to the model.

Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Early and accurate prediction is crucial for reducing mortality. However, clinical settings often face challenges such as data scarcity, class imbalance, and the underutilization of unstructured clinical notes. Existing scoring systems and traditional machine learning models primarily rely on structured vital signs, failing to capture the rich semantic risk factors embedded in textual data. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in text understanding, their high computational costs and potential hallucinations hinder direct deployment in resource-constrained emergency settings. To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel Dual-Teacher Knowledge Fusion (DTKF) framework. First, we introduce a semantic feature augmentation module that leverages DeepSeek to extract semantic risk probabilities from clinical notes and explicitly fuses them with structured vital signs to construct high-order hybrid features for the student model. Second, to prevent overfitting under small-sample conditions, we design a dual-source knowledge distillation strategy. This strategy integrates rule-based knowledge and data-driven semantic knowledge to construct hybrid teacher signals, regulating a lightweight logistic regression student model via soft-label supervision. Experiments on the MIMIC-IV dataset demonstrate that DTKF achieves an AUC of 0.796. This result not only achieves a higher AUC than traditional unimodal baselines but also improves performance by 6.6% compared to direct prediction using LLMs. This study effectively integrates rule-based and data-driven knowledge, enhances feature representation using textual information, and improves model performance and robustness through distillation techniques, providing a clinically valuable solution for sepsis early warning.

The v1.0 record reported a preregistered benchmark of Squirrel OS's Dual Mesh deterministic resolution layer: the in-process mesh resolver resolved synthetic anomalies at a median of 0.000443 ms versus 4509.1 ms for the identical resolution task through an LLM conversation loop (ratio 1.018e+07, n=200/20), with mesh ingestion integrity (50/50 unique collision hashes) and resolution correctness (72/72 replay, zero false positives) verified. Version 2.0 adds a cross-platform verification appendix. The same frozen corpus (sha256 13295d197be59dd1266814bc2f961f1e55e974c61c642fd9c7a6a389668fee59) was re-run under a second preregistered protocol: (1) mesh parity re-run confirming run-over-run determinism (200/200, median 0.00039 ms); (2) the LLM baseline leg re-executed from a second host (Cloudflare Workers edge, 20/20 valid, median 7.386 s, ratio 1.894e+07); and (3) the same task issued to an external LLM API substrate (OpenRouter, deepseek-chat, 20/20 valid, median 179.4 ms, ratio 4.60e+05). The mesh lookup outperforms both substrates on every measured host. The platform-loop wall-clock is shown to be dominated by conversation orchestration rather than model inference (~41x difference). All amendments (host swap, output-fence normalization, rate-limit retry policy) were committed to the public ledger before the respective execution or re-attempt; strict first-pass scores are reported alongside normalized scores, and all raw runs are preserved verbatim in the evidence bundle. Claims remain scoped to the measured environments; no universal performance claim is made. All test data are synthetic; no production, customer, or personal data are involved. This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. It is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All systems are experimental and may contain defects on them.

This systematic review evaluates the effectiveness, diagnostic accuracy, and implementation outcomes of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted screening tools for depression and anxiety in primary care settings, with a focus on literature published since the advent of advanced large language models. A systematic search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and Cochrane Central from January 2020 to September 2025. Ten studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising randomized controlled trials, pragmatic trials, and validation studies. Included studies demonstrated that AI-assisted tools (including conversational chatbots, machine learning models using voice and behavioral data, and digital decision-support systems) can achieve high diagnostic accuracy, with balanced accuracy up to 88.2% and Area Under the Curve (AUC) up to 0.82. Clinically, AI-assisted interventions were associated with higher depression remission (e.g., 27.3% vs. 12.0%) and better anxiety outcomes than treatment-as-usual in individual trials. Feasibility and acceptability were generally favorable, with completion rates often exceeding 60-70% and user satisfaction reaching 79%, even among older adults. Key challenges included limited external validation, demographic homogeneity, and insufficient reporting on ethical safeguards. AI-assisted screening tools show potential to improve the detection and management of depression and anxiety in primary care, with encouraging accuracy, clinical effectiveness, and user engagement in the available studies. However, the evidence base is small and heterogeneous, and future research needs to address gaps in generalizability, long-term efficacy, ethical oversight, and seamless workflow integration to ensure equitable and responsible implementation.

documents.abstract: Adolescents in low- and middle-income countries continue to face substantial barriers in accessing effective HIV education, despite global efforts in prevention. This study evaluated the effectiveness of a culturally adapted HIV educational video developed using artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted video production tools. The intervention assessed in this study was the educational video itself rather than direct interaction with a generative AI system. A quasi-experimental design with pre- and posttests and a control group was used to evaluate the intervention among 60 high school students. Participants were randomly assigned to either a group that received a 10-min AI-generated educational video or a control group that received no intervention. The video was designed to improve HIV health literacy by addressing four domains: access to information, comprehension of core concepts, evaluation of risks, and application of knowledge in real-life decisions. Quantitative data were collected in May 2024 using a validated scale and analyzed with nonparametric tests and analysis of covariance. Students who received the AI-assisted educational video demonstrated significantly higher posttest HIV health literacy scores than the control group (Mann–Whitney U = 206.5, p < .001). After adjustment for baseline scores, analysis of covariance confirmed a significant group effect ( F (1,57) = 21.70, p < .001, partial η 2 = 0.28), indicating a large adjusted effect size. The findings highlight the potential of generative AI as an innovative, scalable tool for adolescent health education, particularly in resource-limited settings. This approach may offer new opportunities for integrating digital strategies into school-based health promotion programs.

Abstract With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), AI-assisted tools are increasingly integrated into language education. However, empirical evidence on their effectiveness for spoken English in higher vocational colleges remains limited. This quasi-experimental study examined whether AI-assisted speaking practice using iFLYTEK Spark, a generative AI platform with speech recognition and real-time feedback capabilities, was associated with higher post-intervention spoken English performance among 92 first-year vocational college students in China. Two intact classes were assigned to an experimental group ( n = 46) receiving 12 weeks of AI-assisted practice plus conventional instruction and a control group ( n = 46) receiving conventional instruction only. Post-intervention speaking performance was assessed by three trained raters using an analytic rubric covering pronunciation, language use, fluency and coherence, and interaction. The experimental group achieved significantly higher overall posttest scores (M = 3.69, SD = 0.76) than the control group (M = 3.19, SD = 0.82; t(90) = 3.011, p = 0.003, Hedges’ g = 0.63). Medium-to-large effect sizes were found in language use (g = 0.49), fluency and coherence (g = 0.50), and interaction (g = 0.75), whereas the difference in pronunciation was smaller and non-significant (g = 0.38, p = 0.071). Semi-structured interviews with one teacher and three students provided supplementary insights into perceived benefits, including increased practice opportunities, reduced speaking anxiety, and enhanced motivation. While the intact-class design and coarse baseline proficiency measure limit causal claims, the findings suggest that AI-assisted tools can serve as a valuable supplement to conventional spoken English instruction in higher vocational settings. Implications for pedagogy and future research directions are discussed.

Humans are more commonly relying on the assistance of advanced robots in decision-making processes and may follow robots’ suggestions depending on their understanding of how such suggestions are generated. To enhance human understanding, robots can communicate their (simulated) intentions, influencing the trust placed upon them. However, it remains uncertain whether and under what conditions robots’ simulated intentions could also negatively impact trust and compliance. Therefore, we conducted a laboratory experiment with 182 participants, exploring whether information about a robot’s potential benevolent intentions and ulterior motives increased or decreased trust and compliance with the robot’s suggestions, while also altering participants’ involvement levels in a decision task. The results of two 2x2x2 ANOVAs revealed that, regardless of the involvement level, the robot’s simulated ulterior motives decreased trust and compliance, while benevolent intentions did not significantly affect these outcomes. Thus, simulated intentions should be considered in the design of collaborative decision-making between humans and robots.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption in logistics depends not only on technological capability but also on employees’ willingness and ability to use AI-based systems. This study examines the factors influencing employees’ behavioural intention to use AI in logistics operations through the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). A positivist, deductive, quantitative and cross-sectional survey design was used in a state-owned energy distribution enterprise in Sri Lanka. The population comprised 93 employees, with 75 targeted and 63 usable responses obtained. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, Pearson correlation and multiple regression in SPSS. Performance expectancy, effort expectancy and facilitating conditions had statistically significant positive effects on behavioural intention, whereas social influence was not statistically significant. Facilitating conditions had the strongest standardized effect (β = 0.326, p = 0.008). The regression model explained 67.0% of the variance in behavioural intention (R² = 0.670). The findings highlight the importance of organisational readiness, practical support, system usability and visible performance benefits when introducing AI into regulated logistics operations. The study contributes context-specific evidence from a state-owned energy distributor in Sri Lanka while recognizing that the single-organization, cross-sectional design limits broader generalization.
