documents.abstract: While autonomous driving technology reduces the operational burden on drivers, it may also diminish their sense of engagement, for example, by interrupting social interactions between drivers and other road users such as pedestrians. To address this, this article proposes a “Social Cooperation” driving mode from a cooperative driving perspective, aiming to activate drivers’ social capabilities to compensate for the limitations of autonomous systems in social interaction and to enhance drivers’ engagement in pedestrian-yielding scenarios. Through a driving simulator prototype experiment, we found that the proposed approach significantly improved drivers’ psychological need satisfaction, enhancing their autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs, while also showing positive trends in empathy, benevolence, and overall satisfaction. The results provide new insights into social interactions in autonomous driving contexts and offer practical and theoretical guidance for the design of human-machine cooperative driving interfaces.

Abstract Large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) systems, especially large language models (LLMs), face growing constraints related to energy use, power delivery, memory traffic, experimentation, and infrastructure capacity. These pressures are often studied separately, which makes it difficult to understand how they interact across the full AI lifecycle. This review develops a cross-layer framework that brings these constraints together and examines whether resource-allocation strategies observed in human cognition can inform more sustainable AI design. We compare human and artificial systems by function rather than anatomy, focusing on how each allocates limited resources to learning, search, memory, external support, optimization, and inference. Using a systematized narrative-review approach, we identified 6284 records, screened 898 at the full-text stage, and selected an initial set of 150 focal studies for detailed synthesis. We organize the evidence into seven interacting regimes covering scaling, experimentation, hardware power limits, data movement, infrastructure, evaluation incentives, and inference allocation. The framework extends Green AI by linking these layers and translating insights from human cognition into testable design hypotheses and measurable evaluation criteria. The strongest near-term opportunities include data selection, energy-aware experimentation, hardware-supported low-precision computation, and demand-adaptive inference. However, most reported gains are based on proxy measures such as operations, memory, latency, or data volume rather than direct end-to-end energy measurements. Near- and in-memory computing show longer-term promise, while retrieval, tool use, distributed experts, and multi-agent systems may shift or increase energy costs through communication and repeated inference. These findings support cross-layer co-design and end-to-end evaluation at matched capability, reliability, latency, and service quality.

Structural health monitoring (SHM) through vibration analysis is essential for ensuring safety, reliability, and minimized maintenance costs in sensor-connected environments. Realizing this at the extreme edge, directly on sensor nodes, requires advanced data analytics, ultra-energy-efficient hardware, and high-fidelity datasets. This paper addresses these challenges by developing an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based deep learning framework for vibration-based structural health monitoring tailored to resource-constrained devices. We present a benchmarking dataset for vibration SHM, encompassing nine abnormal conditions that capture narrowband structural anomalies. Leveraging this dataset, we design supervised and unsupervised deep-learning models, integrating a system identification (SysId) preprocessing stage to derive structurally informed features that enhance model input quality. This improves algorithmic results while boosting hardware performances. These models are deployed on a parallel ultra-low-power microcontroller with dedicated hardware acceleration. Our unsupervised anomaly detectors deliver 89.90 percent (%) accuracy, 4.1 percentage points higher than the state-of-the-art attention-based baseline, favoring recall and missed-detection reduction at the cost of a higher false-alarm rate while consuming 13 microjoules (µJ) in low-power mode and requiring 370 microseconds (µs) in high-performance mode. This marks one of the first experimental validations of unsupervised on-device vibration diagnostics. Supervised counterparts achieve 96.06 % binary and 91.5 % multiclass accuracy, rivaling Residual Network (ResNet) with 15.8 × fewer parameters, at less than 235 µJ and not more than 6.3 ms (ms) inference. Relative to existing edge implementations, our approach is one to three orders of magnitude more energy-efficient and two orders faster, unlocking AI-enabled autonomous, low-latency predictive maintenance for large-scale distributed infrastructure monitoring.

Abstract Precision agriculture is one of the major breakthroughs which has been adopted to counteract some of the major challenges facing contemporary agriculture, such as maximizing crop yield, maximizing resource efficiency, and sustainability. The application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) technologies can go a long way in enhancing crop yield prediction through data obtained from multiple sources, including satellite images, ground sensors, and weather stations. This research paper proposes a next-generation crop yield prediction system called Geo-Optimized Deep Learning (GODL) algorithm. The GODL algorithm integrates geospatial information with deep learning algorithms for crop yield analysis and prediction. This combination of deep learning and geospatial data allows accurate and scalable crop yield predictions using geospatial and sensor information. In order to ensure model optimization in terms of accuracy and efficiency, the GODL Algorithm makes use of advanced hyperparameter optimization methods that include Adam and Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). The research paper highlights the efficiency of the GODL Algorithm by conducting extensive experiments that compare the algorithm’s performance with other crop yield prediction models like Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) and other machine learning techniques. The evaluation takes into consideration important metrics such as accuracy, Jaccard Index, Fowlkes-Mallows Index (FMI), and G-mean, as well as IoT data delay and its effects on the prediction accuracy. In future research, the use of blockchain technology to facilitate data sharing and edge computing to process the data will be considered.

The use of digital tools has enabled the capture of clinical data that can be leveraged to produce real-world evidence, complementing traditional trial data and addressing evidence gaps in oncology. Electronic health records offer rich, longitudinal data, although recording practices, collection methods, and quality may vary over time and across settings, which can lead to inconsistencies. Data harmonization is key to overcoming fragmentation, and common data models offer structured methods for unifying diverse health care data. Various mapping strategies standardize data balancing, automation, flexibility, and semantic precision: ‘upstream semantic mapping' emphasizes standardization, ‘downstream semantic mapping' allows tailored adjustments by local experts, and ‘direct dataset mapping' focuses on creating analysis-ready datasets without intermediate data transformation. The best approach depends on organizational needs, data characteristics, and intended use cases, but harmonization must be a continuous process that adapts to evolving data sources, variable data types, new collection methods, and shifting transformation practices. Clinical expertise must ensure that cohorts mirror real-world scenarios and capture local nuances, more often with an artificial intelligence–assisted framework, while epidemiologists must consider harmonization practices in the study design and analysis. Data strategies must protect patient privacy while supporting health care improvements, with secure data handling paired with accessible sharing. By engaging medical professionals at every stage, health care institutions can become learning health systems driven by high-quality observational research, ultimately advancing knowledge and improving patient outcomes.

Conventional library management systems have serious flaws in finding books and ways of traversing the books and hence it takes more time to search and less satisfaction to users. The incorporation of the artificial intelligence algorithms offers prospects to maximize path finding and the resource location in smart libraries structures. The paper applied A* path finding algorithm in a smart library management system which included use of heuristic functions in calculating optimal route and mapping of books. Three library settings in different layouts with different amounts of collections were used to test the system in terms of the efficiency of retrievals, navigation accuracy, and the time of interaction between the user and the system over a six months span. The A* improved system recorded 94.7 percent accuracy in identifying the location of a book, an efficiency in average retrieval period of 68.3 percent, and a 82.1 percent enhancement of efficiency in navigation as opposed to the traditional system. The score of user satisfaction rose by 91.2 percent and the average system response time is 1.3 seconds. A* algorithm is one of the best algorithms that are used in the enhancement of library navigation facilities, which offers huge advantages in accuracy and effectiveness in retrieval of library information and in whose system current and modern smart library applications are used.

Despite scientific argumentation being a fundamental competency of the PISA assessment framework, prospective biology teachers often demonstrate insufficient development in evidence-based reasoning and rebuttal construction skills. Considering the limitations of large-scale implementation of individualized approaches in higher education, this study evaluates the effectiveness of Generative Artificial Intelligence (ChatGPT-4) configured as a “Socratic tutor” in developing argumentation skills among future educators. An 8-week quasi-experimental study involving 124 students from a pedagogical university employed traditional peer discussion methods in the control group ( n = 62), while the experimental group ( n = 62) utilized an AI agent that induced cognitive dissonance regarding socio-scientific issues. Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) of data obtained through Toulmin's Argument Pattern (TAP) and PISA rubrics confirmed that the experimental group achieved statistically significantly higher overall argumentation quality compared to the control group (F (1,121) = 14.23, p < .001, η 2 = .105). Particularly, participants who received AI-assisted instruction showed marked improvement in forming rebuttals and evaluating counterevidence, which are considered among the most cognitively demanding components within the PISA scientific literacy framework (OECD). These findings suggest that a Generative AI-mediated Socratic instructional package can be an effective and scalable approach for developing epistemic cognition, and they propose a pedagogical model for integrating structured AI-based tutoring into teacher preparation systems aligned with international assessment standards. These findings should be interpreted as evidence for the effectiveness of the structured, AI-mediated Socratic instructional package as a whole, rather than as evidence of AI's inherent superiority over other methods; the relative contribution of the AI medium versus the structured pedagogical protocol it delivers was not directly tested in this design.

This article analyzes the pedagogical potential of integrating differentiated instruction with modern digital technologies in the context of general secondary education, taking into account students’ individual educational needs, level of knowledge, pace of learning, and cognitive abilities. It substantiates the potential for increasing the degree of individualization of the educational process through the integration of traditional forms of differentiated instruction with digital educational tools, adaptive learning systems, educational platforms, electronic assessment, multimedia resources, and artificial intelligence-based technologies.

igital transformation expands access to government, financial, educational, and commercial services, but at the same time increases organizations’ dependence on information systems, network services, cloud platforms, and external providers. Under these conditions, cybersecurity should be viewed not merely as a set of technical safeguards, but as a system of continuous risk management that ensures data confidentiality, integrity, and availability; process resilience; the protection of data subjects’ rights; and business recovery following incidents. The purpose of this article is to systematize the main threats and cybersecurity measures, compare international statistical indicators, and propose a multi-level practical model for commercial organizations and government agencies. This study is based on an analysis of documents from the International Telecommunication Union and the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity, as well as reports from Verizon and IBM, and on a comparative and systematic analysis of approaches to cyber threat management. The data indicate that system vulnerabilities, ransomware, third-party risks, and the human factor remain key elements of the threat landscape. At the same time, the published metrics were obtained using various methodologies and cannot serve as a unified assessment of the frequency of global attacks. The article presents a model that integrates management, prevention, detection, response, and recovery. It was concluded that effective cybersecurity requires clearly measurable goals, the allocation of responsibilities, the protection of supply chains, regular practical exercises, and respect for privacy and other human rights. Keywords: cybersecurity, cyber threat, risk management, incident, data protection, resilience, supply chain, incident response measures

Over the past few decades, organizations have systematically shifted from fragmented, function-specific software tools toward integrated enterprise architectures, with Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) serving as the central technological backbone and a codified model of organizational operations. As contemporary digital transformation and artificial intelligence (AI) adoption accelerate, these emerging capabilities build directly upon established ERP backbones and enterprise data infrastructures rather than operating on a blank slate. This chapter synthesizes three closely related domains—enterprise systems, data management, and ERP—to establish a cohesive, stable conceptual framework and vocabulary for researchers and practitioners. The authors examine the evolutionary trajectory of ERP from 1960s Materials Requirements Planning (MRP) to contemporary multi-tenant cloud and Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) environments. Core operational architectures and functional modules—such as finance, human resources, procurement, manufacturing, and supply chain management—are analyzed alongside essential data management mechanisms. The chapter emphasizes that enterprise integration depends fundamentally on robust data governance, master data management (MDM), and interoperability through middleware and application programming interfaces (APIs) to prevent errors from propagating across business units. Implementation dynamics are explored through the lens of business process reengineering (BPR), technology-organization-environment frameworks, and post-implementation success factors, demonstrating that organizational alignment outweighs purely software-centric considerations. Crucially, the study identifies key theoretical and practical tensions inherent in enterprise digital architectures, including the conflict between system standardization and customization, the concentration of systemic security risks within unified data repositories, and the shift of ERP from a passive system of record to an active, AI-driven system of action. Special attention is devoted to advanced algorithmic transformations, including predictive analytics, process automation, and second-order agentic AI systems capable of executing multi-step autonomous tasks. The authors contend that agentic AI and Industry 4.0 integrations amplify, rather than eliminate, core requirements for data quality, explainability, and explicit decision accountabilities. Ultimately, the chapter concludes that rigorous data governance, strategic change management, and realistic expectations regarding process standardization remain necessary prerequisites for unlocking sustained organizational value from enterprise systems.

The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) into academic inquiry has triggered an unprecedented paradigm shift in educational research. While AI-augmented literature synthesis, automated data coding, and language refinement offer remarkable productivity gains, they simultaneously introduce profound epistemic and methodological vulnerabilities. This doctoral dissertation provides an exhaustive, critical literature review exploring the complex interplay among Epistemic Trust, Methodological Opacity, and Hallucination Risks in modern educational scholarship. Synthesizing extensive peer-reviewed literature published between 2020 and 2024, this study adopts a virtue epistemology framework to analyze how algorithmic cognitive offloading impacts scholarly rigor. The findings reveal a growing systemic tension between productivity acceleration and epistemic vigilance: heavy reliance on generative tools correlates with a decline in primary-source verification, increased vulnerability to algorithmic hallucinations, and an over-reliance on opaque "black-box" data interpretations. Furthermore, this study evaluates current institutional policy responses across international higher education frameworks, highlighting a critical deficit in systematic verification protocols and doctoral AI literacy training. To resolve these systemic vulnerabilities, this review formulates the Epistemic Verification and Transparency Protocol (EVTP), providing actionable guidelines for researchers, journal editors, and university ethics committees to preserve scholarly integrity in an increasingly automated academic landscape.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study investigated equity in the availability and utilization of Artificial Intelligence (AI) facilities among urban and rural public secondary schools in Benue State, Nigeria. The study was guided by two research questions and two hypotheses. A descriptive survey design was adopted. The population comprised 3,726 teachers in 128 public secondary schools, from which 361 teachers were selected using stratified random sampling. Data were collected using the Equitable Utilization of Artificial Intelligence Questionnaire (EUAIQ), validated by three experts in the Faculty of Education, Veritas University, Bwari, Abuja. The instrument yielded a Cronbach’s alpha reliability coefficient of 0.88 based on a trial test involving 30 teachers. Mean and standard deviation were used to answer the research questions, with a 2.50 decision criterion, while independent-samples t-test was used to test the hypotheses at the 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed significant differences between the mean ratings of respondents from urban and rural public secondary schools regarding both the availability and utilization of AI facilities for teaching and learning in Benue State. The study concludes that disparities exist in the availability and utilization of AI facilities between urban and rural public secondary schools. It recommends equitable provision of funding, reliable internet connectivity, stable electricity and AI-enabled digital resources by government and relevant stakeholders, alongside continuous capacity-building programmes for teachers on the effective use of AI facilities.

Artificial intelligence is profoundly reshaping the production and dissemination of digital advertising. Although the content generated by AI has improved the efficiency of creation, it has also caused ethical problems such as false endorsements, hidden advertisements, and algorithm amplification. Based on the ethics of obligation theory, social responsibility theory and utilitarian ethics, this article uses case analysis to critically analyze the phenomenon of ethical misconduct in AI digital advertising. The study found that the platform failed to fully fulfill its public responsibility as a digital communication gater in the process of pursuing commercial interests. This article proposes that the platform should assume the responsibility of algorithm ethics, governance transparency and collaborative governance to rebuild public trust in digital communication.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This chapter provides a critical analysis of the concept of ethics in fashion and the need for moral decision-making as the basis for industry practice. Starting with the definition of ethics and moral philosophy, it examines the use and ambiguities of the terms ‘ethical’ and ‘moral,’ and their use in modern business environments. Central to this chapter is the discussion that ethical decision-making is grounded in human agency and our ability to make choices informed by our values, culture, and experiences. Ethical leadership is influenced by many factors, including personal morals, societal rules, and organisational pressures. These factors can create ethical dilemmas for decision-makers, in which profit and convenience may conflict with what is morally right. The chapter examines the ethical implications of fashion industry practices, including labour exploitation, environmental degradation, animal welfare, transparency, and greenwashing. It highlights the ethical implications of global production systems and examines the role Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) reporting, certifications, legislation, and corporate social responsibility play in making fashion businesses more accountable. It also addresses the emergence of ethical leadership and the role of senior managers in fostering integrity, trust, and ethical decision-making throughout a fashion business. In addition, the chapter will also explore the emerging ethical issues related to Artificial Intelligence, cultural appropriation, diversity and inclusion, and social media and marketing. It will also reflect on ethical consumerism, noting the obstacles consumers face when making purchasing decisions. The chapter will finally discuss why the fashion industry needs to establish ethical business practices to support the transformation to long-term sustainability and increase stakeholder trust.

Abstract: Manual material handling activities on the production line of PT MYR, particularly in the Sugar Vibro, Sugar Grinding, and SSK sections, have the potential to pose a risk of Musculoskeletal Disorders (MSDs), specifically Low Back Pain (LBP). This study aims to evaluate the working posture of production operators, identify the body parts most vulnerable to injury, and formulate recommendations for ergonomic work facilities and methods to reduce injury risk levels and enhance work efficiency. The method used in this study is a combination of the Nordic Body Map (NBM) questionnaire to measure the subjective physical complaints of respondents (n=20) and the Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) method based on digital/photo data processing to objectively evaluate the joint angles of operator postures. The results of the NBM questionnaire data processing indicated that complaints were most dominant in the waist area at 95% (19 out of 20 respondents) and the back area at 75% (15 out of 20 respondents), followed by complaints in the right shoulder (55%) and left shoulder (50%). The posture analysis using the RULA method indicated high to very high ergonomic risk levels: at the Sugar Vibro station, the lifting sacks from pallet activity achieved a final RULA score of 7 (Action Level 4, very high risk), pouring sacks into machine hopper activity achieved a final RULA score of 6 (Action Level 3, high risk), the Sugar Grinding station scored 5 (Action Level 3), and the SSK station scored 7 (Action Level 4). The primary factors contributing to the high LBP risk in operators were the high trunk flexion angle of up to 65°, repetitive lifting of loads weighing 25–50 kg, and static arm and wrist positions without ergonomic support. The proposed improvement recommendations include modifying and redesigning workstations, providing ergonomic material handling equipment, designing work rotation schedules, and conducting regular muscle stretching programs. Keywords: Ergonomics, Nordic Body Map (NBM), Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA), Low Back Pain (LBP), Production Operators, Manual Material Handling. Abstrak: Aktivitas penanganan material secara manual (manual material handling) pada lini produksi PT MYR, khususnya bagian Vibro Gula, Gula Giling, dan SSK, berpotensi menimbulkan risiko cedera otot rangka (Musculoskeletal Disorders/MSDs), khususnya Low Back Pain (LBP). Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengevaluasi postur kerja operator produksi, mengidentifikasi bagian tubuh yang paling berpotensi mengalami gangguan, serta merumuskan usulan perbaikan fasilitas dan cara kerja yang ergonomis guna mengurangi tingkat risiko cedera dan meningkatkan efisiensi kerja. Metode yang digunakan dalam penelitian ini adalah kombinasi kuesioner Nordic Body Map (NBM) untuk mengukur tingkat keluhan fisik subjektif responden (n=20) dan metode Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) berbasis pengolahan data digital/foto untuk mengevaluasi sudut-sudut persendian postur kerja operator secara objektif. Hasil pengolahan data kuesioner NBM menunjukkan keluhan paling dominan dialami pekerja pada area pinggang sebesar 95% (19 dari 20 responden) dan area punggung sebesar 75% (15 dari 20 responden), diikuti oleh keluhan pada bahu kanan (55%) dan bahu kiri (50%). Hasil analisis postur kerja dengan metode RULA mengindikasikan tingkat risiko ergonomi yang tinggi hingga sangat tinggi: stasiun Vibro Gula aktivitas mengangkat karung dari pallet memperoleh skor akhir RULA 7 (Action Level 4, berisiko sangat tinggi), aktivitas menuang karung ke corong mesin memperoleh skor akhir RULA 6 (Action Level 3, berisiko tinggi), stasiun Gula Giling memperoleh skor 5 (Action Level 3), dan stasiun SSK memperoleh skor 7 (Action Level 4). Faktor utama penyebab tingginya risiko LBP pada operator adalah tingginya sudut fleksi pembungkukan batang tubuh (trunk) hingga 65°, pengangkatan beban berulang seberat 25–50 kg, serta posisi lengan dan pergelangan tangan yang menahan beban statis tanpa penopang ergonomis. Rekomendasi perbaikan yang diusulkan meliputi modifikasi dan redesign stasiun kerja, penyediaan alat bantu penanganan material ergonomis, perancangan jadwal rotasi kerja, serta program regangan otot berkala. Kata kunci: Ergonomi, Nordic Body Map (NBM), Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) Low Back Pain (LBP), Operator Produksi, Manual Material Handling.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Evidence synthesis methods, such as systematic reviews (SR), require research teams to find, select, evaluate, and synthesize all available evidence to answer a specific research question in a reproducible and transparent, bias-reduced manner. Early in the process, teams must screen all unique titles and abstracts gathered from a comprehensive search, which can result in thousands of records. Therefore, the process often takes months to years to complete. In this research, we conduct a set of experiments using open-source Large Language Models (LLMs) with small parameters hosted on local servers to screen titles and abstracts against pre-defined eligibility criteria respective to each topic. We use two cases from real SRs for which titles and abstracts screening has already been completed by dual, independent human screeners, which we use as our “ground truth”.

Background As augmented reality (AR) adoption expands across training and operational domains, interaction design has served as a key determinant of user experience (UX). Although natural interaction techniques are believed to better support AR than traditional WIMP (windows, icons, menus, and pointing devices) interfaces, direct comparisons remain limited. Objectives This study compared natural and WIMP-based interaction paradigms in an individual, high-stakes procedural AR training task to evaluate their effects on usability, workload, presence, and task performance. Methods Thirty participants completed a within-subjects experiment using both interaction paradigms in a Tactical Combat Casualty Care AR training scenario delivered on a Meta Quest 3. Condition order was counterbalanced. Subjective outcomes included the System Usability Scale, NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX), and Presence Questionnaire. Objective measures included task completion time, navigation errors, missed procedural steps, corrective actions, requests for clarification, and observed interaction smoothness. Paired-samples t -tests were used to compare conditions, with exploratory analyses examining order effects and relationships between immersive tendency and presence. Results Natural interaction produced significantly higher usability ( p = 0.009) and presence ( p = 0.001) than the WIMP interface. Participants also committed fewer navigation errors, missed fewer procedural steps, required fewer corrective actions, and demonstrated smoother interactions ( p < 0.05) in the natural condition. No significant differences were observed for workload, task completion time, clarification requests, or observed efficiency. An order effect indicated lower perceived workload during participants’ second session, regardless of interaction condition, suggesting a learning effect. Conclusion Natural interaction improves usability, presence, and interaction quality in individual, high-stakes procedural AR training while minimizing execution errors, although it does not necessarily improve speed or decrease cognitive workload during initial use. This evidence suggests that the principal benefits of natural interaction lie in improving the overall UX quality rather than maximizing efficiency, providing guidance for the design of future AR training systems.

OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the quality, safety, and citation characteristics of OpenEvidence across pediatric subspecialties. METHODS: Guideline-anchored clinical questions spanning high, moderate, and low evidence certainty across 6 pediatric subspecialties were submitted to OpenEvidence. Expert reviewer pairs independently scored responses using the validated Quality Analysis of Medical Artificial Intelligence (QAMAI) instrument (6-30 range, higher scores indicate better quality) and a modified Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality harm assessment (0-7 range, higher scores indicate more harm), followed by consensus reconciliation. Citation analysis examined overlap with guideline references, claim substantiation, and pediatric specificity. Response consistency was assessed across 5 repeated queries. RESULTS: Seventeen questions were evaluated. The median QAMAI score was 27/30 (IQR, 24-29; "very good" quality). Potential harm was low (median 0/7, range 0-3), though 6 of 17 responses carried nonzero harm potential. OpenEvidence cited the primary guideline in 15 of 17 questions, yet only 17.6% of responses showed strong citation overlap (≥75% shared references) with the corresponding guidelines. OpenEvidence's citations reliably supported the claims they accompanied (88.2% with high substantiation), and 70.8% of reviewer assessments rated the evidence base as comparable in quality to that of the corresponding guidelines. In total, 35.3% of responses cited studies lacking pediatric specificity. Responses were clinically consistent across repeated queries (77.9% had no meaningful or only minor variation); no contradictory recommendations were observed. CONCLUSIONS: OpenEvidence produced high-quality responses with low expert-rated potential for harm across multiple pediatric subspecialties. The pediatric specificity of cited evidence warrants attention, reflecting the broader challenge of applying artificial intelligence tools that are trained on adult-predominant literature to pediatric populations.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: BackgroundInadequate or misleading health information about silicosis can delay diagnosis, reporting, and exposure removal, potentially affecting risk communication and timely occupational health interventions.ObjectiveThis study evaluates the reliability, quality, and readability of Large Language Models (LLMs) including ChatGPT (GPT-5), Gemini (2.5 Flash), and Copilot (Smart GPT-5), in answering patient-oriented silicosis questions, focusing on risk communication rather than clinical decisions.MethodsSilicosis-related questions were collected from online forums (September 1-7, 2025), and 25 frequently asked, clinically relevant questions were selected and submitted to the LLMs (September 8-14, 2025). Two occupational medicine specialists/pulmonologists independently evaluated responses (September 15-30, 2025) for reliability, quality, and readability using modified DISCERN, Global Quality Scale, and readability indices. Analyses used SPSS version 31.0.ResultsThe LLM-generated responses demonstrated fair reliability. Median (min-max) scores were 23 (12-27) for ChatGPT, 21.5 (14-29) for Gemini, and 26 (17.5-31) for Copilot. Copilot scored significantly higher than ChatGPT and Gemini (p = 0.014). GQS scores were similar across models (p = 0.102), with median scores of 4 (3-5) for ChatGPT and Copilot and 4 (2-5) for Gemini. Readability levels corresponded predominantly to secondary or tertiary education, with no significant differences between the models (all p > 0.05).ConclusionLLMs may enhance worker awareness but have limitations in accuracy and readability. They should complement, not replace, expert-supervised occupational health services. Future studies should align LLMs with international standards, improve accessibility, and establish governance frameworks for transparent and equitable AI use in occupational health.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Automated severity grading of knee osteoarthritis (KOA) has progressed from handcrafted descriptors to deep networks, ordinal objective, attention mechanism and multimodal learning, and explainable artificial intelligence. The source presentation motivating this review focuses on fusion of complementary structur-al and textural radiographic evidence and hybrid learning and interpretable predic-tion. It is well supported recently in literature but some persistent problems can be noted: the classes are not equally sized, the separation of adjacent Kellgren–Lawrence (KL) grades are challenging, performance of the model can be below external validation, and the quality of the explanations is not measured quantita-tively. In this review, we categorize the methods used for grading KOA into handcrafted/radiomics, convolutional and transfer-learning systems, ordinal or hi-erarchical models, transformer and vision–language and fusion-oriented pipe-lines. According to comparative analysis, the contributions of architecture alone are hard to interpret, as there is a strong influence from composition of datasets, labeling practice, projection, preprocessing and validation design on reported measures. Evidence centered fusion is thus not a single network architecture, but a mixture of complementary representations, ordinally aware predictions, calibra-tion, and clinically grounded XAI. Priority directions for clinically credible de-ployment identified in the review include clinically relevant measures of uncer-tainty, quantitative assessment of the quality of explanations, imaging integrated with clinical or longitudinal evidence, leakage-safe splitting, and multi-center evaluation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly studied for tasks such as medical-image analysis, risk prediction, and clinical decision support. However, strong predictive performance does not by itself show why a model reached a particular conclusion or whether that conclusion is appropriate for a patient. This paper reviews explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods that can make healthcare predictions more understandable to clinicians and other stakeholders. A focused narrative review was conducted using foundational work on local explanations and Shapley-value-based feature attribution, a healthcare-focused review, and World Health Organization guidance on AI ethics. The paper compares model-specific and model-agnostic explanations, with particular attention to LIME, SHAP, and visual explanation methods. The review indicates that explanations can support error analysis, communication, and model auditing, but they should not be treated as proof that a prediction is correct, fair, or clinically safe. Explanation quality depends on data quality, model behaviour, the intended user, and the clinical context. The paper proposes a practical evaluation framework combining predictive performance, explanation fidelity, stability, clinical usefulness, fairness checks, and human oversight. It concludes that XAI should be integrated into the full lifecycle of clinical AI systems rather than added only after model development. Index Terms—Explainable AI, healthcare, clinical decision support, interpretability, SHAP, LIME.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Despite showing great skills in working with unstructured data and generating appropriate answers, large language models (LLMs) cannot be applied in critical settings due to their lack of transparency and susceptibility to hallucination. The paper describes an approach to creating explainable LLM-based decision support systems, which includes breaking down complex questions into small subtasks that are processed via auditable pipelines. The approach employs retrieval-augmented generation along with domain-specific knowledge bases and computational instruments for the purpose of producing explanations and demonstrating intermediate reasoning steps while emphasizing data limitations. The approach is tested on clinical decision support problems for a multiple myeloma population. Comparing the results with those obtained when using monolithic LLMs as well as explainable machine learning approaches proves that structured decomposition leads to better decision traceability while achieving similar performance.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Conspectus Catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability arise from coupled electronic, structural, interfacial, transport, and spin-related processes. Conventional catalyst design has relied largely on electronic effects, strain or stress engineering, active-site construction, and local reaction environment control. Although these strategies have enabled major advances, they do not fully capture the spin degrees of freedom associated with open-shell transition-metal centers and magnetically responsive catalysts. Spin state, spin polarization, magnetic moment, spin density, and magnetic ordering can influence adsorbate binding, transition-state stabilization, charge transfer, and reaction pathways, yet their catalytic consequences are often grouped under the broad label of magnetic enhancement without a clear mechanistic assignment. In this Account, we develop explicit spin regulation as a framework for magnetism-informed catalysis. Magnetic enhancement describes an observed response to a magnetic field, a magnetic component, or a magnetic environment. Explicit spin regulation, by contrast, requires deliberate modulation of spin-related variables at or near catalytically active sites and a mechanistic connection to catalytic function. We organize this framework around two routes. Catalyst-integrated spin levers use promoters, interfaces, or interphases to tune the active-site spin/electronic structure, whereas field-induced spin levers introduce external fields or catalyst-localized magnetic perturbations during catalysis. Although implemented differently, both routes seek to control how the active-site spin governs adsorption, transition-state energetics, charge transfer, selectivity, stability, and durability. Our studies provide representative evidence for this framework. Promoter-induced spin modulation stabilizes the N–N dissociation transition state beyond conventional electrostatic promotion, establishing the spin-promotion effect as a catalyst-integrated design principle. In electrocatalysis, external fields, embedded nanomagnets, and magnetic proximity effects provide progressively localized perturbations that can be connected to spin-sensitive active sites, key intermediates, or local magnetic ordering. These examples also show why performance enhancement alone is insufficient. A convincing assignment should connect the imposed perturbation, the active-site spin/electronic response, the affected intermediate or transition state, and the resulting catalytic consequence. Magnetic measurements, electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, element-specific X-ray spectroscopies, operando methods, kinetic analysis, and spin-polarized theory provide complementary elements of this evidence loop. Building on this mechanistic framework, we further translate the active-site spin into catalyst-design descriptors. The local metal-center spin moment can be correlated with oxygen-intermediate adsorption and activity trends, enabling descriptor-guided screening of dual-atom catalysts. Spin-related variables may also inform stability and durability through their connections to phase stability, surface reconstruction, active-site preservation, dissolution resistance, and long-term operation. Generalizing these insights requires paired, standardized, and machine-readable datasets that connect magnetic perturbations, active-site structures, spin-sensitive measurements, catalytic metrics, and durability under comparable conditions. Artificial intelligence-assisted literature mining, knowledge graph construction, high-throughput spin-polarized calculations, active learning, and magnetism-aware machine-learning interatomic potentials may help identify transferable spin descriptors and extend spin-regulated catalyst design to dynamic interfaces. The broader aim is to move magnetism-informed catalysis from phenomenological enhancement toward predictive control through deliberate regulation of the active-site spin.

Background Emotional intelligence is a core competency for nursing students; however, traditional nursing education faces challenges in fostering emotional intelligence, including curricular imbalances, limited teaching methods, and delayed assessment and feedback. The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new possibilities for addressing the above issues; however, existing research has not yet thoroughly explored how nursing students learn emotional intelligence through GenAI or their experiences in this process. Objective Based on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and the Teaching Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, and using Goleman’s five-dimensional model of emotional intelligence as a reference, this study explores the experiences of undergraduate nursing students in using generative artificial intelligence for emotional intelligence learning, as well as the factors that facilitate this process. Method This study employed a qualitative descriptive research design and Reflexive Thematic Analysis (RTA). Using purposive sampling, 19 undergraduate nursing students (from freshman to senior year) were selected for one-on-one semi-structured in-depth interviews. All participants had experience using GenAI tools (such as DeepSeek and Doubao) for communication practice, case discussions, or sentiment analysis. The interview data were analyzed using the RTA six-stage process, with NVivo 12.0 software used to assist with data management. Results We identified and synthesized 238 initial codes into three core themes. Theme 1, “From Efficiency-Driven to Precise Empathy,” presents the differing descriptions of empathy-related experiences among students in different grade levels: lower-grade students more frequently reported efficiency-driven usage experiences; some middle-grade students described difficulties caused by technical barriers; and upper-grade students more often described the recognition of patients’ emotions in conjunction with clinical experience. Theme 2, “From Mimicking AI to Autonomous Expression,” focuses on students’ reported experiences related to social skills, including direct application, recognition and adjustment, autonomous expression, and the simulation gap that persisted throughout the process. Theme 3, “From Technical Frustration to Mental Rehearsal,” integrates experiences related to self-management, self-awareness, and self-motivation. The three themes correspond to different dimensions of emotional intelligence, with students in different grade levels reporting distinct experiential characteristics. Conclusion Nursing undergraduates in different grades exhibit distinct experiential characteristics when using generative artificial intelligence to learn about emotional intelligence. Students’ reports repeatedly highlighted moderate tension around technological motivation, the ability to critically integrate technology, and the perceived value of technological friction. Based on these exploratory findings, we propose several preliminary educational implications—including grade-level-specific support, curriculum exploration, and education in critical technological literacy and ethics—for consideration in future research and practice.

documents.abstract: Abstract This paper presents findings from an ethnographic study of online fashion reselling, an understudied form of gig work where individuals sell secondhand clothing on marketplace platforms. Unlike gig work models where labor is explicitly priced as a service, reselling embeds labor in the procurement, preparation, and sale of goods. We focus on Poshmark, a popular marketplace with 30 million US users, to examine how it mediates reseller labor within broader gendered, classed, and racialized dynamics of precarious work and fashion consumerism. Drawing on infrastructure studies, we extend the concept of torque to analyze how platforms structure reseller experiences across aesthetic, temporal, and regulatory dimensions. Through ethnographic narratives, we illustrate how Poshmark’s sociotechnical mechanisms shape experiences and aspirations of this kind of gig work. Our findings contribute to platform labor research by foregrounding intersectional pressures in marketplace platform work, expanding current understandings of gig economies beyond service work.

This study pursues two objectives. Empirically, it examines how legislative exclusion is produced in South Africa and how gig workers experience it in their everyday working lives. Theoretically, it develops an interpretive account of the relationship between political and economic processes that are ordinarily treated as separate domains, reading political and regulatory exclusion as constitutive of the forms of economic insecurity and precarity that participants describe rather than as their determinant. The study is framed by the concept of legislative exclusion, understood as the process through which state action constitutes a category of workers as falling outside the scope of labor law; precarity, platform capitalism and algorithmic management are used to elaborate the processes through which that exclusion operates and the conditions with which it is associated. A qualitative phenomenological design was adopted. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 purposively sampled gig workers in Johannesburg working across e-hailing, delivery, freelancing and content creation, and the data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The sample spans two structurally distinct segments of platform labor, which are analyzed separately throughout: location-based work (e-hailing and delivery), which is geographically tethered, capital-intensive for the worker and in principle regulable by the national state; and remote online work (digital freelancing and social media content creation), which is contracted across borders and mediated by clients and monetization programs rather than by dispatch algorithms. The analysis reads exclusion as actively produced rather than merely absent: a statutory definition of the employee that platform work is arranged to fall outside, a jurisdictional architecture that renders the responsible corporate entity difficult to reach, and a recent transport regulation that recognizes e-hailing while leaving the employment relationship untouched. These instruments do not bear on the two segments equally: the transport regulation reaches location-based drivers alone, whereas remote online workers are addressed by no domestic instrument at all. Exclusion is in turn bound up with unbounded working hours, exclusion from employment benefits and the absence of any accessible dispute-resolution forum, though it is lived differently in each segment. Location-based participants described unreviewable deactivation and the transfer of vehicle, fuel and licensing costs; online participants described client non-payment, unenforceable informal agreements and dependence on opaque monetisation and visibility rules. The study contributes an interpretive account in which legislative exclusion is understood as a structuring condition through which risk is transferred to workers, platform and client authority is rendered unreviewable, and disadvantage is compounded over time.

Background/Objectives: Integrating Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Realities into Digital Mental Health Services presents novel opportunities for clinical assessment, therapeutic intervention, and continuous rehabilitation. Grounded in dynamic capabilities and sociotechnical systems theories, this study evaluates strategic pathways for integrating Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Realities into Digital Mental Health Services, analyzes core bioethical and data privacy challenges, and examines the prospective impact of immersive virtual environments on patient engagement and therapeutic outcomes. Methods: An iterative three-round Delphi inquiry was conducted with an international panel of 36 multidisciplinary experts spanning clinical psychiatry, Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Realities software development, digital ethics, and healthcare policy. Standardized, neutral visual scenarios prompted expert evaluations across 14 Digital Mental Health Services sub-areas. Panel consensus, rating dispersion, and domain interrelationships were quantified using Kendall’s coefficient of concordance (W), non-parametric Spearman rank-order correlation analysis, and descriptive dispersion metrics (median, interquartile range, standard deviation), complemented by reflexive thematic qualitative synthesis. Results: Expert agreement converged significantly from Round 1 to Round 3. High consensus emerged for AI-enhanced initial screening (mean = 4.7, SD = 0.5) and comprehensive VR assessments (mean = 4.5, SD = 0.8). While AI-managed crisis services showed high perceived probability (95%), findings highlighted the necessity of strict human-in-the-loop architectures over full autonomy to mitigate psychiatric triage hazards. Conclusions: Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Realities present viable adjunctive pathways for personalized psychiatric assessment and therapy, provided that systems implement strict clinician-in-the-loop safeguards, real-time dynamic consent, and end-to-end data encryption. Utilizing a Dynamic Capabilities framework enables healthcare organizations to systematically sense technological innovations, seize clinical opportunities, and reconfigure governance structures, thereby ensuring equitable, safe, and ethical digital mental health delivery.

documents.abstract: Abstract Large language models are increasingly embedded in clinical decision support, but they are stateless. They preserve no epistemic commitments across contexts, identical cases can yield divergent outputs, and fluent generation can acquire de facto authority over what counts as evidence without any matching structure of responsibility. We argue that whether clinical AI can be trusted and held accountable depends on where epistemic authority sits and who governs it, not on how well the model performs or how fluently it generates. From this it follows that epistemic governance has to be externalized from the model. It also has to be constrained, because relocating authority into a second generative layer reproduces the original problem. We make the claim concrete with a non-agentic, constraint-based architecture, instantiated in oncology. Context classification, evidence authority, and truth-state assignment are settled by dedicated, inspectable layers before any generation occurs; the language model is confined to bounded extraction and summarization. The central move is to keep deontic authority, what is permitted and reimbursed, distinct from epistemic authority, what the evidence supports, so that a reimbursement or jurisdictional constraint is represented as an allocation decision rather than collapsed into an apparent clinical fact. Uncertainty, disagreement between authoritative sources, and clinician overrides are preserved as explicit, inspectable states. By settling authority before generation and keeping it inspectable, the architecture restores the structure of responsibility that fluent generation erodes: the exercise of authority becomes attributable, and the resulting recommendation can be contested rather than absorbed as plain clinical fact.

documents.abstract: Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Claude have rapidly permeated higher education, fundamentally altering the ways in which students learn, conduct research, and prepare for careers. Despite their widespread availability, the extent to which students adopt these tools varies considerably, influenced by factors such as perceived usefulness, ease of use, AI literacy, trust, and ethical awareness. This study investigates the determinants of AI tool adoption among 300 undergraduate and postgraduate students and examines the association between AI tool adoption and perceived employability skills. Employing a quantitative, survey-based research design with a structured five-point Likert scale questionnaire, data were analysed using multiple linear regression, simple linear regression, and independent samples t-test. The multiple regression model explained 34.1% of the variance in AI adoption (R² = 0.341, F(5, 294) = 30.4, p < .001), with AI literacy emerging as the strongest predictor (β = 0.304, p < .001), followed by perceived ease of use (β = 0.269), trust in AI (β = 0.269), perceived usefulness (β = 0.263), and ethical awareness (β = 0.164). The simple regression demonstrated that AI adoption significantly predicted employability skills (R² = 0.349, β = 0.591, p < .001). Furthermore, postgraduate students exhibited significantly higher AI adoption levels than undergraduate students, t(298) = 2.74, p = .007, with a small effect size (Cohen’s d = 0.334). These findings underscore the necessity for educational institutions to integrate AI literacy training and responsible AI usage policies into curricula, thereby equipping students with the digital competencies demanded by AI-driven workplaces. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI adoption in higher education by integrating multiple adoption determinants within a single empirical framework and linking them to employability outcomes.

Orientation: Digital technologies, particularly artificial intelligence (AI), are rapidly transforming human resource functions by enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of human resource practices. Research purpose: This systematic review examines the factors that facilitate the integration of AI into global talent management (GTM) and explores how these factors collectively inform theory on technology-enabled talent management systems. Motivation for the study: Research on the use of AI in GTM remains limited, and its theoretical implications are not yet well established. Research approach/design and method: A systematic literature review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews framework. The review encompassed eight databases (Google Scholar, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, ProQuest, Emerald Insight, Sabinet and Elsevier) using a comprehensive and structured search strategy. Peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2020 and 2025 were screened. Twenty-three empirical studies meeting the inclusion criteria were subjected to full-text analysis. Main findings: The analysis revealed that AI integration into GTM is influenced by several interconnected enablers, including the strategic alignment of AI with talent objectives, adequate capabilities and digital infrastructure, ethical and governance frameworks and organisational readiness for implementation. Practical/managerial implications: Human resources practitioners and policymakers should adopt a systemic, integrative approach that aligns AI tools with organisational talent objectives. Contribution/value-add: This review advances theoretical discourse by integrating fragmented evidence into a cohesive understanding of the conditions that support AI-driven GTM. It offers a conceptual foundation for future research seeking to build theory at the intersection of AI, GTM and strategic human resource management.

The article provides a comprehensive analysis of the use of generative artificial intelligence (hereinafter – AI) in the creation of visual advertising content and its impact on contemporary marketing practices in Ukraine and abroad. It is demonstrated that the integration of AI-generated photo and video materials transforms not only the set of advertising tools but also the very logic of organizing the advertising process, reshaping the balance between creative, managerial, and technological components. Generative models form a new type of creative environment in which content production becomes fast, flexible, and data-driven, allowing for scalability without a proportional increase in the costs. The study systematizes the key areas of application of generative AI in advertising, including the personalization of visual messages, production optimization, the development of dynamic formats, and the use of data-driven storytelling. At the same time, it is identified that technological advantages are accompanied by a number of risks related to the standardization of creative solutions, dependence on the quality of input data and on external technological infrastructure, the weakening of brand distinctiveness, and an increased likelihood of ethical and legal violations. It is argued that in the absence of adequate managerial control, generative content may lose strategic alignment with brand positioning and the long-term objectives of the enterprise. Special attention is paid to the Ukrainian context, which is characterized by the combination of rapid adoption of AI solutions with human resource, institutional, and regulatory constraints intensified by wartime conditions. It is shown that under these circumstances generative artificial intelligence performs a dual role: on the one hand, it acts as a tool for improving the effectiveness of marketing communications; on the other hand, it requires clearly defined frameworks for responsible use. The article concludes that generative AI should be viewed as a driver of structural change in the advertising industry, the effectiveness of which depends on its integration into marketing management systems, the quality of managerial decision-making, compliance with ethical principles and legal requirements, and the ability of brands to maintain their distinct character.

University libraries are critical campus venues characterized by high-density occupancy, making comprehensive fire evacuation safety assessment essential for protecting lives and cultural assets. Conventional evaluation methods often suffer from either subjective bias or a lack of engineering realism, while standalone cloud models lack robust weight allocation mechanisms. To address these deficiencies, this study proposes a fire evacuation safety evaluation method integrating combined weighting and the cloud model. An evaluation framework consisting of 21 indicators is established across four dimensions: human factors, evacuation facilities, emergency management, and venue environment. For weight determination, the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) and the entropy method are synthesized to balance expert experience with data-driven objectivity. The cloud model is then employed to handle the inherent fuzziness and randomness in safety assessment, utilizing the forward and backward cloud generators to map qualitative linguistic descriptions to quantitative values based on three digital characteristics: expectation (Ex), entropy (En), and hyper-entropy (He). A case study of a university library in Wuhan is conducted. The results demonstrate that the library’s overall fire evacuation safety level is "Excellent," with a comprehensive cloud parameter set of (83.577, 0.620, 0.116). The assessment reveals that while evacuation facilities perform optimally, the complex architectural layout represents a structural vulnerability, and personnel safety literacy requires further stabilization. This integrated framework effectively overcomes the limitations of single-weighting strategies and provides a reliable, fine-grained quantitative tool for fire safety management and targeted risk mitigation in high-density public buildings.

A review of literature on Quality-Orientation (QO) and Firm Innovativeness (FI) on Firm Performance (FP), It identifies the importance of usage of each principal of Quality Orientations and Firm innovativeness by usage of emerging technology for consistent firm performance. We also review the generalizability of Quality Management Principles (QMP) and Innovativeness as mediating and moderating constructs on Firm Performance. This study identifies the gaps in firm innovativeness by reviewing Intent to innovate and usage of emerging technologies in a Firm. We also reflect the generalizability of innovativeness and usage of emerging technology tools, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learnings, and Robotics process automation as effective variables on firm performance. Future implications on Firm Innovativeness on firm performance for further research.

Maintaining a consistent and effective fitness routine requires more than simply following predefined exercise plans, as users often struggle with incorrect exercise form, inadequate personalization, nutritional decision-making, and the lack of continuous feedback. Recent advances in computer vision, deep learning, pose estimation, and artificial intelligence have enabled automated systems for exercise recognition and form assessment. However, many existing fitness applications address these capabilities independently and provide limited integration between exercise monitoring, nutritional analysis, and personalized coaching. This paper presents FitCoach, an AI-assisted fitness coaching system designed to provide an integrated and personalized fitness experience using computer vision and intelligent decision-making. The proposed system utilizes human pose estimation to identify body landmarks and analyze exercise movements, enabling real-time assessment of exercise form and feedback. In addition, the system incorporates food recognition and nutritional information to support dietary monitoring, while user-specific information is considered to generate more personalized fitness recommendations. The system is designed to combine multimodal inputs, including visual exercise information, user activity, and nutritional data, into a unified coaching framework. By integrating exercise-form analysis, dietary awareness, and personalized guidance, FitCoach aims to overcome limitations of isolated fitness technologies and provide users with accessible, adaptive, and intelligent fitness support. The proposed framework demonstrates how computer vision and AI-based personalization can be combined to develop a more comprehensive digital fitness coaching solution.

Foundation models (FMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as a transformative paradigm in artificial intelligence, reshaping the landscape of medical image analysis and clinical decision support. Building upon large-scale pretraining on heterogeneous datasets, these models exhibit unprecedented generalization and zero-shot transfer capabilities, effectively overcoming the perennial bottleneck of annotated data scarcity that has historically constrained deep learning applications in healthcare. This review paper presents the state of the art in FMs and VLMs applied to medical imaging, encompassing a broad spectrum of modalities including radiography, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), pathology whole-slide images, ophthalmology, dermatology, and echocardiography. A structured taxonomy of architectures, training strategies, and adaptation mechanisms is provided, covering contrastive learning (CLIP-based), generative, and hybrid paradigms. Also, seminal works are critically analyzed, such as MedCLIP, BioViL, BiomedCLIP, MedSAM, SAM-Med2D, LLaVA-Med, Med-PaLM 2, CONCH, and BiomedGPT, examining their methodological contributions, benchmark performance, and inherent limitations. Additionally, research gaps are discussed, including insufficient 3D volumetric understanding, limited multimodal reasoning in rare disease contexts, translational barriers for clinical deployment, and critical ethical concerns such as algorithmic bias and privacy. Further, emerging trends are presented encompassing instruction-tuned multimodal large language models (LLMs), agent-based systems, federated learning, and FMs for time-series physiological data. Finally, research directions are highlighted for clinically validated, equitable, and deployable AI systems in medical imaging.

documents.abstract: Many modern scientific studies record more variables than observations. A single experiment may measure thousands of quantities while collecting only hundreds of samples. Inthis regime the classical multivariate toolbox stops working. Principal component analysis,the standard tool for keeping the few strongest patterns of a table of data, loses its guarantees, and so do Gaussian graphical models, which map the direct links between variables,mixture models, which describe data that come from a few hidden groups, and robust estimators, which are built to resist outliers. Deep learning, meanwhile, does very well here. This survey explains why, structure by structure. It first arranges the mathematical foundations into seven layers, from matrix algebra to inference and validation, and traces each deep architecture to the layers that power it. It then reviews the classical theory and its five characteristic failure modes, and shows when depth escapes the curse of dimensionality and how much data is saved when a known symmetry is built into a network. The core of the survey is a taxonomy built on structural assumptions: each deep architecture autoencoders, graph neural networks, attention and state-space models, normalizing flows, diffusion, flow matching, deep clustering, robust autoencoders – is paired with the classical method it extends. Foundation models, which are pretrained once and then applied to a new dataset in a single forward pass, are shown to generalize empirical Bayes shrinkage. A synthesis records, guarantee by guarantee, what classical theory survives in the deep extensions, what weakens, and what is lost. Benchmark evidence, applications, and six open problems complete the survey.

Background Artificial intelligence (AI) has demonstrated high diagnostic performance in skin cancer detection and is increasingly being integrated into clinical workflows. However, whether these advances translate into meaningful patient-relevant and healthcare system outcomes remains unclear. Evidence on value-oriented outcomes has not been systematically synthesized. Methods We conducted a PRISMA-ScR–guided scoping review of studies published between January 2015 and October 2025 identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science. Studies evaluating AI-based technologies for skin cancer diagnosis, triage, risk stratification, or management were included if they reported outcomes beyond technical performance metrics. Reported outcomes were mapped to three value-oriented domains: clinical and prognostic, process and experiential, and system-level and economic outcomes. Results Of 4,021 records identified, 33 studies met the inclusion criteria, whereas 389 publications were excluded because they reported only technical performance metrics without value-oriented outcomes. Reported outcomes were predominantly process and experiential (28/33 studies), including diagnostic confidence, workflow efficiency, and user acceptance. Clinical and prognostic outcomes were reported in only five studies, with four studies focussing on prognostic utility and one study focussing on patient management, while system-level and economic outcomes were identified in three studies. Most evaluations were conducted in controlled experimental settings, whereas prospective real-world implementation studies were less common. Overall, the available evidence predominantly focused on process-level benefits, with limited evidence for clinical and prognostic or system-level and economic outcomes. Discussion Current evaluation strategies for AI-based skin cancer diagnostics remain predominantly performance-oriented and are largely focused on process and experiential outcomes. From a value-based healthcare perspective, current evidence remains largely confined to intermediate stages of the diagnostic value chain: although AI-assisted systems may improve diagnostic workflows, clinician confidence, and clinical decision making, few studies have evaluated their impact on downstream patient-relevant clinical and prognostic, or system-level and economic outcomes. Future research should prioritize prospective real-world studies, outcome-driven evaluation frameworks, and economic assessments that examine the impact of AI-supported decision-making on clinical outcomes and healthcare systems. Conclusion Despite promising effects on diagnostic processes, evidence for the clinical and system-level value of AI-based skin cancer diagnostics remains limited. Outcome-driven evaluation frameworks are needed to bridge the gap between algorithmic performance and meaningful healthcare impact.

documents.abstract: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes have achieved rapid and widespread clinical adoption, with early evidence suggesting trainees derive disproportionate benefit compared to other clinician groups. Yet the outcomes measured so far - documentation time, cognitive workload, clinician burnout - speak to the value of these tools for workforce sustainability rather than for medical education. Physician practice is shifting from authoring clinical notes to editing AI-generated ones, and trainees are inheriting that shift without a defined competency for performing it. Here, we argue that reviewing AI-generated clinical documentation is a teachable competency that current curricula are not yet designed to develop, and that simulation-based education is well-suited to both teach the competency and produce the developmental evidence the clinical literature has yet to produce.

documents.abstract: The increasing availability of large-scale consumer data and advances in computational technologies have transformed marketing into a data-driven discipline. Mathematical and computational frameworks play a critical role in supporting decision-making processes by enabling organizations to analyze complex market dynamics, predict consumer behavior, optimize resource allocation, and improve strategic planning. This study has four objectives: to characterize the intellectual structure of the field, to classify the mathematical and computational methods employed and the marketing functions to which they are applied, to examine emerging technological developments, and to identify research and methodological gaps. A systematic literature review was conducted, reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines and organized through the Literature Review based on Systematic Bibliometry (LRSB) protocol. A single, fully documented query executed in Scopus returned 56 records, of which 45 met the eligibility criteria and were retained for both bibliometric science mapping and qualitative synthesis. The corpus spans 1992–2025. The review examines the integration of mathematical modeling, optimization techniques, machine learning algorithms, simulation methods, and data analytics within contemporary marketing practices. Drawing on the interdisciplinary convergence of marketing, engineering, mathematics, and computer science, the paper examines how computational approaches enhance market segmentation, customer engagement, demand forecasting, pricing strategies, advertising performance, and customer relationship management. The analysis highlights the growing relevance of predictive and prescriptive analytics in converting raw data into actionable insights that support evidence-based managerial decisions. Furthermore, the study discusses emerging trends, including artificial intelligence, real-time analytics, and intelligent decision support systems, that are reshaping the marketing landscape. The review also documents families of decision-support methods that are well established in the wider literature but almost absent from the retrieved corpus—multi-criteria decision making, mathematical programming beyond the linear case, metaheuristic optimization and Bayesian decision models—and treats this absence as a substantive research gap. Challenges related to data quality, model interpretability, computational complexity, and ethical considerations are also addressed. The findings suggest that the effective integration of mathematical and computational frameworks can significantly improve organizational competitiveness by increasing decision accuracy, operational efficiency, and responsiveness to market changes. This research contributes to a broader understanding of how advanced analytical methods support the transition from data collection to strategic decision-making in modern marketing environments.

While many individuals with this persistent infеctiоn may not show symptoms, it саn lead to сhrоnic gastritis and peptic ulсеrs. Furthermore, there is a strong link between H. pylori and the development оf gаstric аdenоcarcinоma as well as mucоsa-assосiated lymphoid tissue lymphoma. The increasing resistance tо antimicrobial agents has significantly hindered successful eradiсаtiоn еffоrts and underscored the necessity for improved diаgnоstiс and treatment methods. This review offers a critical analysis of the global inequalities in H. pylori infеctiоn ratеs, the challenges posed by antimicrobial resistance, issues with current diаgnоstiс practices, strategies for еradicatiоn, and new therаpеutiс devеlоpmеnts. We pаrticularly highlight the role of molecular diagnostics, suсh as drоplеt digital PCR and whоle-gеnоme sequencing, due to their capacity to swiftly detect mutations assоciаtеd with resistance and facilitate tailored treatment plans.
